332	4.5 No fresh post-t0 squats (negative control)
333	
334	Of the 2,000 extra generations, 11 produced a name that was absent from our snapshot yet live at
335	check time. Adjudicated by registration date, all 11 predate t0 by years (2014 to 2023); they are
336	names our unreliable npm snapshot missed, not post-t0 squats. This is a negative control over a
337	window of only a few days, and is essentially uninformative about whether attackers will register
338	these names going forward; that is a question for the prospective watch (Section 7), not a finding
339	we lean on.

343	
344	The registration data says almost no one is claiming these names. It says nothing about whether
345	the underlying primitive works. We confirm that it does, in a sealed environment, using only our

347	to any index) whose only effect is to print a banner and write a single marker file. We install it

398	6 Limitations
399	
400	We are explicit about what this does and does not show.
401	
402	• Zero malicious is not zero risk. The attack primitive works, and a benign proof-of-concept
403	  under a hallucinated name has drawn tens of thousands of installs in prior work. Our finding is
404	  that, in this sample and window, the registered names are not malicious, not that a weaponized
405	  one could not spread. “Benign now” is also version-scoped: a placeholder can be weaponized in
406	  a later release under the same name.
407	• The registered census is small and biased. The taxonomy rests on 22 registered names
408	  from a 149-name anchor drawn from public lists, which defenders preferentially scrape. It is a
409	  snapshot of publicly-listed names, not a population estimate, and the intent labels were assigned
410	  by one adjudicator against a fixed rubric.
411	• Lower-bound corpus. Because the npm snapshot has false inclusions, some real hallucinations
412	  are rejected before a live check. The 1,641 is a floor.
413	• Self-generated, not production traﬀic. Our corpus comes from our own prompts to open-
414	  weight models. It is a controlled proxy for what agents emit in the wild, not a capture of live
415	  agent traﬀic.
416	• Short window. Whether these names get claimed going forward needs calendar time that a
417	  single snapshot cannot provide.
418	
419	
420	7 Future work
421	
422	We keep the dated 1,641-name corpus under a prospective watch and intend to re-check it periodi-
423	cally to see how many names, and in which category, are claimed over time; the value grows as that
424	forward window lengthens. The natural next step is to move from our self-generated corpus toward
425	live coding-agent traﬀic, so the exposure measurement reflects what developers actually run, and
426	to negotiate access to larger gated corpora that are not pre-filtered by public visibility.

429	8 Conclusion
430	
431	Hallucination is common and does not saturate: five open-weight models invent new plausible
432	package names about as fast as we can sample them. But inventing a name is exposure, not harm.
433	When we follow the names to the registry, two things hold in this data. The names our own models
434	invent are essentially unclaimed: all 1,641 remain unregistered by anyone. And among hallucinated
435	names that have circulated publicly and been registered, none are malicious; the registered set is
436	dominated by one anonymous benign-placeholder operation. The slopsquatting threat is genuine
437	in principle, and worth defending against, but the measured registration reality is, so far, quiet.
438	The contribution is a method and a set of numbers anyone can move: if the malicious count rises,
439	this same pipeline will catch it.

755	B. Extracting package names from generated code
756	To identify package hallucinations, we first need to reliably extract package references from model-generated code. We
757	implement language-specific extractors using regular expressions that capture the idiomatic package import patterns of

759	For each supported language, we identify and extract the following reference patterns:

762	       – Direct imports (import package name)
763	       – Qualified imports (from package name import ...)

765	  • JavaScript: The extractor handles both modern ECMAScript modules and CommonJS patterns:

767	       – CommonJS requires (require(’package name’))

<!-- Frontmatter: single-line values; they feed literature-matrix.md via `rlab index`.
     status: draft (in progress) -> ready (analyst self-check passed) -> complete (critical review passed).
     evidence_basis: full-text | abstract-only. abstract-only analyses must not fill methodology detail.
     relevance: high | medium | low. -->

# We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs

- Authors: Spracklen, Joseph; Wijewickrama, Raveen; Sakib, A H M Nazmus; Maiti, Anindya; Viswanath, Bimal; Jadliwala, Murtuza
- Year / venue: 2024, arXiv (preprint), analysed version arXiv:2406.10279v3, 2 Mar 2025 (p. 1). Published version: USENIX Security 2025. This is stated by the project lead and by the reference lists of two other project papers ([@churilov2026range, p. 16]; [@okwor2026hallucination, p. 9]). The arXiv text does not itself name the venue, so we analysed the arXiv text and cannot rule out differences from the proceedings version.
- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2406.10279 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10279
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
[A] The paper aims to quantify how prevalent package hallucinations are in Python and JavaScript code produced by commercial and open-source code LLMs, how model settings affect them, what the hallucinated names look like, and whether mitigation can reduce them without hurting code quality (p. 2, p. 4). The authors call it "the first systematic study" of package-hallucination frequency and nature (p. 2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [A] RQ1: how prevalent are package hallucinations in Python and JavaScript code generated by LLMs? (p. 4)
- [A] RQ2: how do model settings (training-data recency, temperature, decoding strategy) affect them? (p. 4)
- [A] RQ3: what model behaviours are observed: repetition within a model, cross-model repetition, verbosity, and self-detection? (p. 4)
- [A] RQ4: what properties do hallucinated names have: similarity to popular packages, cross-language confusion, and recently deleted packages? (p. 4)
- [A] RQ5: can RAG, self-refinement, decoding strategies or supervised fine-tuning mitigate hallucinations? (p. 4–5)
- [A] Explicit hypothesis on deleted packages: they expected a sizeable share of hallucinations to come from packages removed from PyPI. The hypothesis was not supported (p. 11).
- [A] Adversary model: the attacker can query the same LLMs, cannot modify them, finds hallucinated names by cross-referencing the registry and registers them. Victims install suggested packages without checking them (p. 4).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Three-phase pipeline: (i) build the prompt datasets, (ii) generate code, (iii) detect hallucinations (p. 5). This is followed by targeted sub-experiments for RQ2–RQ4 and a mitigation experiment for RQ5 (p. 7–13).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] 16 models (Table 1): GPT-4, GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-3.5 Turbo; CodeLlama 7B/13B/34B; DeepSeek Coder 1.3B/6.7B/33B; Magicoder 6.7B; WizardCoder 34B; Mistral 7B; Mixtral 8x7B; OpenChat 7B; WizardCoder-Python 7B; CodeLlama-Python 33B (p. 6). Selection used the top of the EvalPlus leaderboard as of 20 January 2024 plus the GPT models (p. 5). Two Python-only models were not tested on JavaScript, which gives 30 tests (p. 6).
- Package-name extraction: [V] Three heuristics (p. 6–7):
  - H1: parse `pip install` / `npm install` commands that appear in the output without being requested (7% of outputs).
  - H2: give the generated code back to the same model and ask for the list of packages needed to run it.
  - H3: give the original prompt back to the same model and ask which packages would solve the task.

  The authors explicitly reject parsing `import` / `require` because module names do not map uniquely to package names (p. 6, Appendix G p. 19).
- Hallucination decision: [V] A name is a hallucination if it is absent from a master list of PyPI or npm package names taken on 10 January 2024 (p. 7). [A] Because the master list may already contain squatted names, the authors present their rates as a lower bound (p. 7).
- Mitigation: [V] Three approaches, each tested alone and as an ensemble, on DeepSeek Coder 6.7B and CodeLlama 7B (p. 12–13):
  - RAG: 65,000 statements of the form "Package [x] could answer questions about [y]", generated with LlaMA-2 from the top 20,000 PyPI packages, stored in a vector DB, top-5 retrieved and appended to the prompt.
  - Self-refinement: the model is asked whether its packages are valid and regenerates up to 5 times.
  - Supervised fine-tuning: on 560,000 valid-only H1/H2 response pairs.
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Commercial vs open-source models; Python vs JavaScript; "recent" (2023) vs "all-time" (pre-2023) prompt subsets (p. 5, p. 7–8); temperature sweep and top-p/top-k/min-p settings (p. 8); unmitigated baseline vs each mitigation (p. 13). [V] They also compare their results with Lanyado's blog estimate (GPT-3.5 24.2%, GPT-4 22.2%) (p. 7).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] Stack Overflow dataset (p. 5):
  - 240 manually selected tags, each with more than 5,000 questions and relevant to Python or JavaScript.
  - The 20 most-upvoted questions per tag give 4,800 prompts per language.
  - This is done twice, once for 2023 ("recent") and once for before 2023 ("all-time"), giving 9,600 prompts per language.

  [V] LLM-generated dataset (p. 5):
  - Descriptions of the 5,000 most-downloaded PyPI and npm packages were turned into one-sentence coding prompts by Llama-2 70B (prompt template in Figure 13, p. 19).
  - About 4,800 prompts per language.
  - Also split into recent and all-time halves, with overlap removed.
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 19,200 code samples per model-language test, 30 tests, 576,000 code samples in total (p. 6). Two package prompts per sample give 1,152,000 package prompts (p. 7). These produced 2.23 million package mentions, of which 440,445 were hallucinated and 205,474 were unique hallucinated names (p. 7). [V] The paper also gives 19,500 prompts and 586,000 samples in the contributions list (p. 2), which does not match the 576,000 elsewhere (p. 1, p. 6). The source of this discrepancy is not reported.
- Sampling / selection method: [V]
  - RQ2–RQ4 use only Python, 4 models (GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-3.5, CodeLlama 7B, DeepSeek 6.7B) and "randomly sampled subsets" of the datasets (p. 7). The subset sizes are not reported, except for 500 prompts in the persistence test (p. 9).
  - Self-detection used randomly sampled valid and hallucinated names; the sample size is not reported (p. 9–10).
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Code, both prompt datasets, generated code, the RAG database and the fine-tuned models are released at Zenodo record 14676377 and GitHub Spracks/PackageHallucination (p. 2, p. 14). [V] The master list of hallucinated names and per-test detailed results are withheld and shared "by request to verified researchers" (p. 14).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
  - [V] Open-source models ran through Hugging Face transformers with GPTQ-quantized weights (p. 6).
  - [V] Hardware (p. 18): a 40-node Debian cluster with A100/V100 GPUs, and an Ubuntu machine with 3 RTX 6000 GPUs.
  - [V] RQ1 parameters (Table 6, p. 19): temperature 0.7 for code generation and 0.01 for package prompts; top-p 0.9; top-k 20; repetition penalty 1; max tokens 2048 for code and 64 for package prompts.
  - [V] System messages and prompts are given verbatim in Figures 10–13 (p. 18–19).
  - [V] Temperature sweep: up to 2 for GPT models and up to 5 for open-source models (p. 8).
  - [V] Decoding settings: top-p 0.4/0.6/0.8, top-k 5/10/15, min-p 0.1/0.2/0.3, plus one combined setting. Top-k and min-p were tested only on the open models (p. 8).
  - [V] Registry ground truth: PyPI and npm master lists as of 10 January 2024 (p. 7). Deleted packages were found with Google BigQuery PyPI download counts from 2022 and earlier (p. 11). Cross-language checks used libraries.io lists for 9 registries (p. 11).
  - **Name normalisation** (case folding, PEP 503 `-`/`_`/`.` equivalence, npm scopes): not reported.
  - **Standard-library exclusion**: not reported.
  - **Deduplication rule**: rates count mentions. "Unique" names are distinct strings (p. 7). The exact rule is not reported.
- Code availability: [V] Yes, see section 4 (p. 14).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - [V] Package hallucination rate = number of hallucinated packages / total recommended packages (p. 7). This is a mention-level rate. It pools names from H1 (installs inside code) and H2/H3 (the model answering a direct "which packages" question).
  - [V] Persistence: how many of 10 re-queries reproduce the same hallucinated name (p. 9).
  - [V] Number of models that generate each unique name (p. 10).
  - [V] Levenshtein distance to the nearest valid package (p. 10–11).
  - [V] Self-detection accuracy, precision and recall (p. 10).
  - [V] HumanEval pass@1 for code quality after fine-tuning (p. 13).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): Not reported. No confidence intervals, significance tests or variance across runs are given. Words such as "significantly reduce" are used descriptively (p. 1, p. 13). [V] The Python–JavaScript relationship is described as "linear" and "positively correlated" from a scatter plot. No coefficient is reported (p. 7, Figure 14 p. 19).

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] Hallucinations are frequent overall: 440,445 of 2.23 million package mentions (19.7%) were hallucinated, including 205,474 unique non-existent names (p. 7).
2. [V] Commercial models hallucinated less than open models: GPT models 5.2% vs open-source 21.7% (p. 7). GPT-4 Turbo had the lowest rate at 3.59%. DeepSeek 1B was the lowest open model at 13.63% (p. 7). Per-model rates ranged up to 26.12% for Python (CodeLlama 7B) and 35.71% for JavaScript (CodeLlama 7B) (Tables 7–8, p. 20).
3. [V] Python hallucinated less than JavaScript: 15.8% vs 21.3% on average (p. 7). Stack Overflow prompts gave higher rates than LLM-generated prompts for almost every model, e.g. CodeLlama 7B Python 32.53% vs 21.51% (Table 7, p. 20).
4. [V] Hallucinations repeat within a model. Over 500 prompts re-queried 10 times each, 43% of hallucinated names reappeared in all 10 runs and 39% never reappeared. 58% reappeared more than once (p. 9).
5. [V] Most hallucinated names are model-specific: 81% of distinct names came from only one model (p. 10).
6. [V] Most hallucinated names are not typos of real packages. Only 13.4% (10,263 of 76,489) are within Levenshtein distance 1–2 of a real package; 48.6% are at distance 6 or more (p. 11).
7. [V] Deleted packages contribute almost nothing: 133 names (0.17%) matched packages removed from PyPI (p. 11). 8.7% (6,705 of 76,489) of hallucinated Python names are valid npm packages (p. 11).
8. [V] Temperature matters. Rates rise with temperature and jump above 1; at maximum temperature GPT-4 reached 8.9% and GPT-3.5 reached 31.8% (p. 8). Changing top-p/top-k/min-p increased rates slightly (+1.16% on average) and did not help (p. 8). Prompts on recent topics gave about a 10% higher rate (p. 8–9).
9. [V] Models can partly recognise their own hallucinations. GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-3.5 and DeepSeek detected them with accuracy above 75%. CodeLlama was biased toward labelling names as valid (Figure 7, Table 2, p. 10).
10. [V] All mitigations reduced hallucination rates (Table 4, p. 13). Fine-tuning reduced code quality: HumanEval pass@1 fell from 51.4% to 25.3% for DeepSeek and from 19.6% to 16.4% for CodeLlama (Table 5, p. 13).

| Condition | DeepSeek 6.7B | CodeLlama 7B |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline | 16.14% | 26.28% |
| RAG | 12.24% | 13.40% |
| Self-refinement | 13.04% | 25.51% |
| Fine-tuning | 2.66% | 10.27% |
| Ensemble | 2.40% | 9.32% |

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] The master list may already contain squatted hallucinated names, so the rates are a lower bound (p. 7).
- [A] RQ2–RQ4 were run only on Python, 4 models and sampled subsets. The authors argue this does not compromise generalisability (p. 7).
- [A] Newer models released since writing may behave differently. Few commercial models were tested because of funding (p. 13).
- [A] Self-refinement may misclassify valid packages as hallucinations (p. 12).
- [A] Fine-tuning reduces code quality (p. 13).
- [A] Removed-package lists are not fully disclosed by registries (p. 3). They did not publish real packages for ethical reasons, so exploitation was not demonstrated (p. 14).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **The metric mixes three name sources.** H2 and H3 ask the model directly for package lists (p. 6–7). Names from these answers are not necessarily names that would be installed from generated code. The pooled mention-level rate is therefore not the same quantity as "hallucinated dependency in code". It is also not comparable with rates computed by import/install parsing (e.g. churilov2026range) or per prompt (krishna2025importing). Based on the heuristic definitions on p. 6–7.
- [I] **Name normalisation and stdlib handling are not reported.** If names were matched without PEP 503 normalisation, case and separator variants of real packages would be counted as hallucinations, which would inflate rates. Based on the absence of any normalisation description on p. 7.
- [I] **Possible train/test leakage in the mitigation results.** Fine-tuning used the 560,000 valid responses produced from the same prompt datasets (p. 12–13). The prompts used to evaluate the fine-tuned models are not described. The 2.66% result may therefore be partly in-distribution.
- [I] **No uncertainty is reported.** Each condition is a single run. Rate differences of a few points (e.g. self-refinement on CodeLlama, 26.28% → 25.51%) cannot be judged without CIs (p. 13).
- [I] **Internal inconsistencies in the text and tables.**
  - 586,000 vs 576,000 samples (p. 2 vs p. 6).
  - CodeLlama is marked "✗" (not open source) in Table 1 (p. 6) but treated as open-source in the text.
  - Malformed counts in Table 7: "(2,495/41,7)" and "(2,8523/13,329)" (p. 20).
  - GPT-4 JavaScript SO cell: 3.86% does not equal 1,672/23,416 = 7.1% (p. 20).
  - The recency effect is phrased in both directions ("10% higher ... for older data versus more recent data" vs the summary "More recent prompting topics lead to a 10% increase", p. 8–9).

  These are probably typos, but they lower confidence in exact numbers.
- [I] **"10%" for recency is ambiguous.** It is not clear whether this means relative change or percentage points (p. 8).
- [I] **No real-world exploitation data.** The registry snapshot (January 2024) predates the analysis, and registrations of the hallucinated names after the run were not tracked (RQ2 gap).

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection):
  - [I] The same model both generates the code and names its packages (H2/H3), so its self-consistency is part of the measurement.
  - [I] Fine-tuning data comes from the same prompt pool used to evaluate it (p. 12–13).
  - [I] The LLM-generated prompts were produced by Llama-2 70B, which belongs to the same family as the CodeLlama models being evaluated (p. 5).
- External (generalisability of sample/context):
  - [I] Models date from 2023–early 2024 (p. 5–6). Agentic tools and IDE assistants are not covered.
  - [V] Only Python and JavaScript are studied (p. 6).
  - [I] Open models were run GPTQ-quantized (p. 6), so the results may not transfer to full-precision weights.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?):
  - [I] "Absent from the 10 Jan 2024 list" is used as a proxy for "hallucinated". The authors acknowledge the contamination direction (p. 7).
  - [I] Normalisation, stdlib handling and private or scoped names are unaddressed (p. 7).
  - [I] Mention-level counting gives more weight to verbose models.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No tests, no CIs, no repeated runs except the 10-run persistence check (p. 9). The large N makes the headline rates stable, but between-condition comparisons are not inferentially supported.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Prompts, system messages and parameters are given in Appendix B/C (p. 18–19), and code and datasets are public (p. 14). [V] The hallucinated-name list is withheld (p. 14). [I] Exact replication of the commercial-model results is impossible because those endpoints have since changed.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A] (p. 13):
  - Find the underlying causes of package hallucination: architecture, tokenizer, training-data composition.
  - Develop mitigations tailored to code: prompt engineering, knowledge graphs, loss refinement, new fine-tuning methods.
  - Add real-time feedback mechanisms.
  - Study persistence at the token level.
  - Develop fine-tuning that keeps code quality (p. 13).
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - Re-measure with an import/install-based extractor and explicit PEP 503 normalisation, so results are comparable with later studies.
  - Evaluate cheap tool-side defences on held-out prompts. Examples: a registry-existence plus package-age/popularity check before install, or self-refinement with a small model.
  - Track whether hallucinated names get registered over time (RQ2).

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (rates by model, language, temperature, recency), RQ2 (persistence, cross-model overlap, similarity to real names), RQ3 (RAG, self-refinement, fine-tuning), RQ4 (prompt sources, registry snapshot, heuristics).
- How it informs our work [I]:
  - **Baseline.** This is the baseline paper and the source of the reusable prompt corpus (public Zenodo/GitHub, p. 14). A laptop-scale study can sample from the SO and LLM-generated prompt sets and stay comparable with both this paper and churilov2026range.
  - **Replication details** (all from p. 5–7 and p. 18–19):
    - prompt sources: Stack Overflow top-20 per tag for 240 tags, 2023 vs pre-2023; Llama-2-70B prompts from top-5,000 package descriptions;
    - system prompts: Figures 10–13;
    - temperatures: 0.7 for code, 0.01 for package prompts;
    - registry snapshot: 10 Jan 2024;
    - metric: hallucinated / all recommended packages;
    - normalisation: not reported. Our study must define it explicitly (PEP 503 for PyPI, lowercase for npm, scoped names kept whole).
  - **Defences.** The two training-free mitigations are laptop-feasible: RAG over a package-description index (13.40% vs 26.28% on CodeLlama) and self-refinement. Self-refinement only helps models that can recognise their own hallucinations (p. 10, p. 13). Fine-tuning is costly and harmed code quality (p. 13).
  - **Persistence.** The 43%/39% split (p. 9) means a measurement study needs several samples per prompt to tell persistent names (worth squatting) from noise.

# We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs

- Authors: Spracklen, Joseph; Wijewickrama, Raveen; Sakib, A H M Nazmus; Maiti, Anindya; Viswanath, Bimal; Jadliwala, Murtuza
- Year / venue: 2024, arXiv (preprint), analysed version arXiv:2406.10279v3, 2 Mar 2025 (p. 1). Published version: USENIX Security 2025. This is stated by the project lead and by the reference lists of two other project papers ([@churilov2026range, p. 16]; [@okwor2026hallucination, p. 9]). The arXiv text does not itself name the venue, so we analysed the arXiv text and cannot rule out differences from the proceedings version.
- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2406.10279 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10279
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
[A] The paper aims to quantify how prevalent package hallucinations are in Python and JavaScript code produced by commercial and open-source code LLMs, how model settings affect them, what the hallucinated names look like, and whether mitigation can reduce them without hurting code quality (p. 2, p. 4). The authors call it "the first systematic study" of package-hallucination frequency and nature (p. 2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [A] RQ1: how prevalent are package hallucinations in Python and JavaScript code generated by LLMs? (p. 4)
- [A] RQ2: how do model settings (training-data recency, temperature, decoding strategy) affect them? (p. 4)
- [A] RQ3: what model behaviours are observed: repetition within a model, cross-model repetition, verbosity, and self-detection? (p. 4)
- [A] RQ4: what properties do hallucinated names have: similarity to popular packages, cross-language confusion, and recently deleted packages? (p. 4)
- [A] RQ5: can RAG, self-refinement, decoding strategies or supervised fine-tuning mitigate hallucinations? (p. 4–5)
- [A] Explicit hypothesis on deleted packages: they expected a sizeable share of hallucinations to come from packages removed from PyPI. The hypothesis was not supported (p. 11).
- [A] Adversary model: the attacker can query the same LLMs, cannot modify them, finds hallucinated names by cross-referencing the registry and registers them. Victims install suggested packages without checking them (p. 4).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Three-phase pipeline: (i) build the prompt datasets, (ii) generate code, (iii) detect hallucinations (p. 5). This is followed by targeted sub-experiments for RQ2–RQ4 and a mitigation experiment for RQ5 (p. 7–13).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] 16 models (Table 1): GPT-4, GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-3.5 Turbo; CodeLlama 7B/13B/34B; DeepSeek Coder 1.3B/6.7B/33B; Magicoder 6.7B; WizardCoder 34B; Mistral 7B; Mixtral 8x7B; OpenChat 7B; WizardCoder-Python 7B; CodeLlama-Python 33B (p. 6). Selection used the top of the EvalPlus leaderboard as of 20 January 2024 plus the GPT models (p. 5). Two Python-only models were not tested on JavaScript, which gives 30 tests (p. 6).
- Package-name extraction: [V] Three heuristics (p. 6–7):
  - H1: parse `pip install` / `npm install` commands that appear in the output without being requested (7% of outputs).
  - H2: give the generated code back to the same model and ask for the list of packages needed to run it.
  - H3: give the original prompt back to the same model and ask which packages would solve the task.

  The authors explicitly reject parsing `import` / `require` because module names do not map uniquely to package names (p. 6, Appendix G p. 19).
- Hallucination decision: [V] A name is a hallucination if it is absent from a master list of PyPI or npm package names taken on 10 January 2024 (p. 7). [A] Because the master list may already contain squatted names, the authors present their rates as a lower bound (p. 7).
- Mitigation: [V] Three approaches, each tested alone and as an ensemble, on DeepSeek Coder 6.7B and CodeLlama 7B (p. 12–13):
  - RAG: 65,000 statements of the form "Package [x] could answer questions about [y]", generated with LlaMA-2 from the top 20,000 PyPI packages, stored in a vector DB, top-5 retrieved and appended to the prompt.
  - Self-refinement: the model is asked whether its packages are valid and regenerates up to 5 times.
  - Supervised fine-tuning: on 560,000 valid-only H1/H2 response pairs.
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Commercial vs open-source models; Python vs JavaScript; "recent" (2023) vs "all-time" (pre-2023) prompt subsets (p. 5, p. 7–8); temperature sweep and top-p/top-k/min-p settings (p. 8); unmitigated baseline vs each mitigation (p. 13). [V] They also compare their results with Lanyado's blog estimate (GPT-3.5 24.2%, GPT-4 22.2%) (p. 7).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] Stack Overflow dataset (p. 5):
  - 240 manually selected tags, each with more than 5,000 questions and relevant to Python or JavaScript.
  - The 20 most-upvoted questions per tag give 4,800 prompts per language.
  - This is done twice, once for 2023 ("recent") and once for before 2023 ("all-time"), giving 9,600 prompts per language.

  [V] LLM-generated dataset (p. 5):
  - Descriptions of the 5,000 most-downloaded PyPI and npm packages were turned into one-sentence coding prompts by Llama-2 70B (prompt template in Figure 13, p. 19).
  - About 4,800 prompts per language.
  - Also split into recent and all-time halves, with overlap removed.
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 19,200 code samples per model-language test, 30 tests, 576,000 code samples in total (p. 6). Two package prompts per sample give 1,152,000 package prompts (p. 7). These produced 2.23 million package mentions, of which 440,445 were hallucinated and 205,474 were unique hallucinated names (p. 7). [V] The paper also gives 19,500 prompts and 586,000 samples in the contributions list (p. 2), which does not match the 576,000 elsewhere (p. 1, p. 6). The source of this discrepancy is not reported.
- Sampling / selection method: [V]
  - RQ2–RQ4 use only Python, 4 models (GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-3.5, CodeLlama 7B, DeepSeek 6.7B) and "randomly sampled subsets" of the datasets (p. 7). The subset sizes are not reported, except for 500 prompts in the persistence test (p. 9).
  - Self-detection used randomly sampled valid and hallucinated names; the sample size is not reported (p. 9–10).
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Code, both prompt datasets, generated code, the RAG database and the fine-tuned models are released at Zenodo record 14676377 and GitHub Spracks/PackageHallucination (p. 2, p. 14). [V] The master list of hallucinated names and per-test detailed results are withheld and shared "by request to verified researchers" (p. 14).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
  - [V] Open-source models ran through Hugging Face transformers with GPTQ-quantized weights (p. 6).
  - [V] Hardware (p. 18): a 40-node Debian cluster with A100/V100 GPUs, and an Ubuntu machine with 3 RTX 6000 GPUs.
  - [V] RQ1 parameters (Table 6, p. 19): temperature 0.7 for code generation and 0.01 for package prompts; top-p 0.9; top-k 20; repetition penalty 1; max tokens 2048 for code and 64 for package prompts.
  - [V] System messages and prompts are given verbatim in Figures 10–13 (p. 18–19).
  - [V] Temperature sweep: up to 2 for GPT models and up to 5 for open-source models (p. 8).
  - [V] Decoding settings: top-p 0.4/0.6/0.8, top-k 5/10/15, min-p 0.1/0.2/0.3, plus one combined setting. Top-k and min-p were tested only on the open models (p. 8).
  - [V] Registry ground truth: PyPI and npm master lists as of 10 January 2024 (p. 7). Deleted packages were found with Google BigQuery PyPI download counts from 2022 and earlier (p. 11). Cross-language checks used libraries.io lists for 9 registries (p. 11).
  - **Name normalisation** (case folding, PEP 503 `-`/`_`/`.` equivalence, npm scopes): not reported.
  - **Standard-library exclusion**: not reported.
  - **Deduplication rule**: rates count mentions. "Unique" names are distinct strings (p. 7). The exact rule is not reported.
- Code availability: [V] Yes, see section 4 (p. 14).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - [V] Package hallucination rate = number of hallucinated packages / total recommended packages (p. 7). This is a mention-level rate. It pools names from H1 (installs inside code) and H2/H3 (the model answering a direct "which packages" question).
  - [V] Persistence: how many of 10 re-queries reproduce the same hallucinated name (p. 9).
  - [V] Number of models that generate each unique name (p. 10).
  - [V] Levenshtein distance to the nearest valid package (p. 10–11).
  - [V] Self-detection accuracy, precision and recall (p. 10).
  - [V] HumanEval pass@1 for code quality after fine-tuning (p. 13).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): Not reported. No confidence intervals, significance tests or variance across runs are given. Words such as "significantly reduce" are used descriptively (p. 1, p. 13). [V] The Python–JavaScript relationship is described as "linear" and "positively correlated" from a scatter plot. No coefficient is reported (p. 7, Figure 14 p. 19).

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] Hallucinations are frequent overall: 440,445 of 2.23 million package mentions (19.7%) were hallucinated, including 205,474 unique non-existent names (p. 7).
2. [V] Commercial models hallucinated less than open models: GPT models 5.2% vs open-source 21.7% (p. 7). GPT-4 Turbo had the lowest rate at 3.59%. DeepSeek 1B was the lowest open model at 13.63% (p. 7). Per-model rates ranged up to 26.12% for Python (CodeLlama 7B) and 35.71% for JavaScript (CodeLlama 7B) (Tables 7–8, p. 20).
3. [V] Python hallucinated less than JavaScript: 15.8% vs 21.3% on average (p. 7). Stack Overflow prompts gave higher rates than LLM-generated prompts for almost every model, e.g. CodeLlama 7B Python 32.53% vs 21.51% (Table 7, p. 20).
4. [V] Hallucinations repeat within a model. Over 500 prompts re-queried 10 times each, 43% of hallucinated names reappeared in all 10 runs and 39% never reappeared. 58% reappeared more than once (p. 9).
5. [V] Most hallucinated names are model-specific: 81% of distinct names came from only one model (p. 10).
6. [V] Most hallucinated names are not typos of real packages. Only 13.4% (10,263 of 76,489) are within Levenshtein distance 1–2 of a real package; 48.6% are at distance 6 or more (p. 11).
7. [V] Deleted packages contribute almost nothing: 133 names (0.17%) matched packages removed from PyPI (p. 11). 8.7% (6,705 of 76,489) of hallucinated Python names are valid npm packages (p. 11).
8. [V] Temperature matters. Rates rise with temperature and jump above 1; at maximum temperature GPT-4 reached 8.9% and GPT-3.5 reached 31.8% (p. 8). Changing top-p/top-k/min-p increased rates slightly (+1.16% on average) and did not help (p. 8). Prompts on recent topics gave about a 10% higher rate (p. 8–9).
9. [V] Models can partly recognise their own hallucinations. GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-3.5 and DeepSeek detected them with accuracy above 75%. CodeLlama was biased toward labelling names as valid (Figure 7, Table 2, p. 10).
10. [V] All mitigations reduced hallucination rates (Table 4, p. 13). Fine-tuning reduced code quality: HumanEval pass@1 fell from 51.4% to 25.3% for DeepSeek and from 19.6% to 16.4% for CodeLlama (Table 5, p. 13).

| Condition | DeepSeek 6.7B | CodeLlama 7B |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline | 16.14% | 26.28% |
| RAG | 12.24% | 13.40% |
| Self-refinement | 13.04% | 25.51% |
| Fine-tuning | 2.66% | 10.27% |
| Ensemble | 2.40% | 9.32% |

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] The master list may already contain squatted hallucinated names, so the rates are a lower bound (p. 7).
- [A] RQ2–RQ4 were run only on Python, 4 models and sampled subsets. The authors argue this does not compromise generalisability (p. 7).
- [A] Newer models released since writing may behave differently. Few commercial models were tested because of funding (p. 13).
- [A] Self-refinement may misclassify valid packages as hallucinations (p. 12).
- [A] Fine-tuning reduces code quality (p. 13).
- [A] Removed-package lists are not fully disclosed by registries (p. 3). They did not publish real packages for ethical reasons, so exploitation was not demonstrated (p. 14).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **The metric mixes three name sources.** H2 and H3 ask the model directly for package lists (p. 6–7). Names from these answers are not necessarily names that would be installed from generated code. The pooled mention-level rate is therefore not the same quantity as "hallucinated dependency in code". It is also not comparable with rates computed by import/install parsing (e.g. churilov2026range) or per prompt (krishna2025importing). Based on the heuristic definitions on p. 6–7.
- [I] **Name normalisation and stdlib handling are not reported.** If names were matched without PEP 503 normalisation, case and separator variants of real packages would be counted as hallucinations, which would inflate rates. Based on the absence of any normalisation description on p. 7.
- [I] **Possible train/test leakage in the mitigation results.** Fine-tuning used the 560,000 valid responses produced from the same prompt datasets (p. 12–13). The prompts used to evaluate the fine-tuned models are not described. The 2.66% result may therefore be partly in-distribution.
- [I] **No uncertainty is reported.** Each condition is a single run. Rate differences of a few points (e.g. self-refinement on CodeLlama, 26.28% → 25.51%) cannot be judged without CIs (p. 13).
- [I] **Internal inconsistencies in the text and tables.**
  - 586,000 vs 576,000 samples (p. 2 vs p. 6).
  - CodeLlama is marked "✗" (not open source) in Table 1 (p. 6) but treated as open-source in the text.
  - Malformed counts in Table 7: "(2,495/41,7)" and "(2,8523/13,329)" (p. 20).
  - GPT-4 JavaScript SO cell: 3.86% does not equal 1,672/23,416 = 7.1% (p. 20).
  - The recency effect is phrased in both directions ("10% higher ... for older data versus more recent data" vs the summary "More recent prompting topics lead to a 10% increase", p. 8–9).

  These are probably typos, but they lower confidence in exact numbers.
- [I] **"10%" for recency is ambiguous.** It is not clear whether this means relative change or percentage points (p. 8).
- [I] **No real-world exploitation data.** The registry snapshot (January 2024) predates the analysis, and registrations of the hallucinated names after the run were not tracked (RQ2 gap).

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection):
  - [I] The same model both generates the code and names its packages (H2/H3), so its self-consistency is part of the measurement.
  - [I] Fine-tuning data comes from the same prompt pool used to evaluate it (p. 12–13).
  - [I] The LLM-generated prompts were produced by Llama-2 70B, which belongs to the same family as the CodeLlama models being evaluated (p. 5).
- External (generalisability of sample/context):
  - [I] Models date from 2023–early 2024 (p. 5–6). Agentic tools and IDE assistants are not covered.
  - [V] Only Python and JavaScript are studied (p. 6).
  - [I] Open models were run GPTQ-quantized (p. 6), so the results may not transfer to full-precision weights.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?):
  - [I] "Absent from the 10 Jan 2024 list" is used as a proxy for "hallucinated". The authors acknowledge the contamination direction (p. 7).
  - [I] Normalisation, stdlib handling and private or scoped names are unaddressed (p. 7).
  - [I] Mention-level counting gives more weight to verbose models.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No tests, no CIs, no repeated runs except the 10-run persistence check (p. 9). The large N makes the headline rates stable, but between-condition comparisons are not inferentially supported.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Prompts, system messages and parameters are given in Appendix B/C (p. 18–19), and code and datasets are public (p. 14). [V] The hallucinated-name list is withheld (p. 14). [I] Exact replication of the commercial-model results is impossible because those endpoints have since changed.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A] (p. 13):
  - Find the underlying causes of package hallucination: architecture, tokenizer, training-data composition.
  - Develop mitigations tailored to code: prompt engineering, knowledge graphs, loss refinement, new fine-tuning methods.
  - Add real-time feedback mechanisms.
  - Study persistence at the token level.
  - Develop fine-tuning that keeps code quality (p. 13).
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - Re-measure with an import/install-based extractor and explicit PEP 503 normalisation, so results are comparable with later studies.
  - Evaluate cheap tool-side defences on held-out prompts. Examples: a registry-existence plus package-age/popularity check before install, or self-refinement with a small model.
  - Track whether hallucinated names get registered over time (RQ2).

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (rates by model, language, temperature, recency), RQ2 (persistence, cross-model overlap, similarity to real names), RQ3 (RAG, self-refinement, fine-tuning), RQ4 (prompt sources, registry snapshot, heuristics).
- How it informs our work [I]:
  - **Baseline.** This is the baseline paper and the source of the reusable prompt corpus (public Zenodo/GitHub, p. 14). A laptop-scale study can sample from the SO and LLM-generated prompt sets and stay comparable with both this paper and churilov2026range.
  - **Replication details** (all from p. 5–7 and p. 18–19):
    - prompt sources: Stack Overflow top-20 per tag for 240 tags, 2023 vs pre-2023; Llama-2-70B prompts from top-5,000 package descriptions;

    - temperatures: 0.7 for code, 0.01 for package prompts;
    - registry snapshot: 10 Jan 2024;

Self-refinement only helps models that can recognise their own hallucinations (p. 10, p. 13). Fine-tuning is costly and harmed code quality (p. 13).

  - **Allow-list argument.** The authors argue that a plain existence check is insufficient because an attacker can pre-register names (p. 12). A lightweight defence should therefore add package age, popularity or provenance signals rather than existence alone.

# We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs

- Authors: Spracklen, Joseph; Wijewickrama, Raveen; Sakib, A H M Nazmus; Maiti, Anindya; Viswanath, Bimal; Jadliwala, Murtuza
- Year / venue: 2024, arXiv (preprint), analysed version arXiv:2406.10279v3, 2 Mar 2025 (p. 1). Published version: USENIX Security 2025. This is stated by the project lead and by the reference lists of two other project papers ([@churilov2026range, p. 16]; [@okwor2026hallucination, p. 9]). The arXiv text does not itself name the venue, so we analysed the arXiv text and cannot rule out differences from the proceedings version.
- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2406.10279 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10279
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
[A] The paper aims to quantify how prevalent package hallucinations are in Python and JavaScript code produced by commercial and open-source code LLMs, how model settings affect them, what the hallucinated names look like, and whether mitigation can reduce them without hurting code quality (p. 2, p. 4). The authors call it "the first systematic study" of package-hallucination frequency and nature (p. 2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [A] RQ1: how prevalent are package hallucinations in Python and JavaScript code generated by LLMs? (p. 4)
- [A] RQ2: how do model settings (training-data recency, temperature, decoding strategy) affect them? (p. 4)
- [A] RQ3: what model behaviours are observed: repetition within a model, cross-model repetition, verbosity, and self-detection? (p. 4)
- [A] RQ4: what properties do hallucinated names have: similarity to popular packages, cross-language confusion, and recently deleted packages? (p. 4)
- [A] RQ5: can RAG, self-refinement, decoding strategies or supervised fine-tuning mitigate hallucinations? (p. 4–5)
- [A] Explicit hypothesis on deleted packages: they expected a sizeable share of hallucinations to come from packages removed from PyPI. The hypothesis was not supported (p. 11).
- [A] Adversary model: the attacker can query the same LLMs, cannot modify them, finds hallucinated names by cross-referencing the registry and registers them. Victims install suggested packages without checking them (p. 4).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Three-phase pipeline: (i) build the prompt datasets, (ii) generate code, (iii) detect hallucinations (p. 5). This is followed by targeted sub-experiments for RQ2–RQ4 and a mitigation experiment for RQ5 (p. 7–13).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] 16 models (Table 1): GPT-4, GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-3.5 Turbo; CodeLlama 7B/13B/34B; DeepSeek Coder 1.3B/6.7B/33B; Magicoder 6.7B; WizardCoder 34B; Mistral 7B; Mixtral 8x7B; OpenChat 7B; WizardCoder-Python 7B; CodeLlama-Python 33B (p. 6). Selection used the top of the EvalPlus leaderboard as of 20 January 2024 plus the GPT models (p. 5). Two Python-only models were not tested on JavaScript, which gives 30 tests (p. 6).
- Package-name extraction: [V] Three heuristics (p. 6–7):
  - H1: parse `pip install` / `npm install` commands that appear in the output without being requested (7% of outputs).
  - H2: give the generated code back to the same model and ask for the list of packages needed to run it.
  - H3: give the original prompt back to the same model and ask which packages would solve the task.

  The authors explicitly reject parsing `import` / `require` because module names do not map uniquely to package names (p. 6, Appendix G p. 19).
- Hallucination decision: [V] A name is a hallucination if it is absent from a master list of PyPI or npm package names taken on 10 January 2024 (p. 7). [A] Because the master list may already contain squatted names, the authors present their rates as a lower bound (p. 7).
- Mitigation: [V] Three approaches, each tested alone and as an ensemble, on DeepSeek Coder 6.7B and CodeLlama 7B (p. 12–13):
  - RAG: 65,000 statements of the form "Package [x] could answer questions about [y]", generated with LlaMA-2 from the top 20,000 PyPI packages, stored in a vector DB, top-5 retrieved and appended to the prompt.
  - Self-refinement: the model is asked whether its packages are valid and regenerates up to 5 times.
  - Supervised fine-tuning: on 560,000 valid-only H1/H2 response pairs.
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Commercial vs open-source models; Python vs JavaScript; "recent" (2023) vs "all-time" (pre-2023) prompt subsets (p. 5, p. 7–8); temperature sweep and top-p/top-k/min-p settings (p. 8); unmitigated baseline vs each mitigation (p. 13). [V] They also compare their results with Lanyado's blog estimate (GPT-3.5 24.2%, GPT-4 22.2%) (p. 7).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] Stack Overflow dataset (p. 5):
  - 240 manually selected tags, each with more than 5,000 questions and relevant to Python or JavaScript.
  - The 20 most-upvoted questions per tag give 4,800 prompts per language.
  - This is done twice, once for 2023 ("recent") and once for before 2023 ("all-time"), giving 9,600 prompts per language.

  [V] LLM-generated dataset (p. 5):
  - Descriptions of the 5,000 most-downloaded PyPI and npm packages were turned into one-sentence coding prompts by Llama-2 70B (prompt template in Figure 13, p. 19).
  - About 4,800 prompts per language.
  - Also split into recent and all-time halves, with overlap removed.
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 19,200 code samples per model-language test, 30 tests, 576,000 code samples in total (p. 6). Two package prompts per sample give 1,152,000 package prompts (p. 7). These produced 2.23 million package mentions, of which 440,445 were hallucinated and 205,474 were unique hallucinated names (p. 7). [V] The paper also gives 19,500 prompts and 586,000 samples in the contributions list (p. 2), which does not match the 576,000 elsewhere (p. 1, p. 6). The source of this discrepancy is not reported.
- Sampling / selection method: [V]
  - RQ2–RQ4 use only Python, 4 models (GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-3.5, CodeLlama 7B, DeepSeek 6.7B) and "randomly sampled subsets" of the datasets (p. 7). The subset sizes are not reported, except for 500 prompts in the persistence test (p. 9).
  - Self-detection used randomly sampled valid and hallucinated names; the sample size is not reported (p. 9–10).
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Code, both prompt datasets, generated code, the RAG database and the fine-tuned models are released at Zenodo record 14676377 and GitHub Spracks/PackageHallucination (p. 2, p. 14). [V] The master list of hallucinated names and per-test detailed results are withheld and shared "by request to verified researchers" (p. 14).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
  - [V] Open-source models ran through Hugging Face transformers with GPTQ-quantized weights (p. 6).
  - [V] Hardware (p. 18): a 40-node Debian cluster with A100/V100 GPUs, and an Ubuntu machine with 3 RTX 6000 GPUs.
  - [V] RQ1 parameters (Table 6, p. 19): temperature 0.7 for code generation and 0.01 for package prompts; top-p 0.9; top-k 20; repetition penalty 1; max tokens 2048 for code and 64 for package prompts.
  - [V] System messages and prompts are given verbatim in Figures 10–13 (p. 18–19).
  - [V] Temperature sweep: up to 2 for GPT models and up to 5 for open-source models (p. 8).
  - [V] Decoding settings: top-p 0.4/0.6/0.8, top-k 5/10/15, min-p 0.1/0.2/0.3, plus one combined setting. Top-k and min-p were tested only on the open models (p. 8).
  - [V] Registry ground truth: PyPI and npm master lists as of 10 January 2024 (p. 7). Deleted packages were found with Google BigQuery PyPI download counts from 2022 and earlier (p. 11). Cross-language checks used libraries.io lists for 9 registries (p. 11).
  - **Name normalisation** (case folding, PEP 503 `-`/`_`/`.` equivalence, npm scopes): not reported.
  - **Standard-library exclusion**: not reported.
  - **Deduplication rule**: rates count mentions. "Unique" names are distinct strings (p. 7). The exact rule is not reported.
- Code availability: [V] Yes, see section 4 (p. 14).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - [V] Package hallucination rate = number of hallucinated packages / total recommended packages (p. 7). This is a mention-level rate. It pools names from H1 (installs inside code) and H2/H3 (the model answering a direct "which packages" question).
  - [V] Persistence: how many of 10 re-queries reproduce the same hallucinated name (p. 9).
  - [V] Number of models that generate each unique name (p. 10).
  - [V] Levenshtein distance to the nearest valid package (p. 10–11).
  - [V] Self-detection accuracy, precision and recall (p. 10).
  - [V] HumanEval pass@1 for code quality after fine-tuning (p. 13).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): Not reported. No confidence intervals, significance tests or variance across runs are given. Words such as "significantly reduce" are used descriptively (p. 1, p. 13). [V] The Python–JavaScript relationship is described as "linear" and "positively correlated" from a scatter plot. No coefficient is reported (p. 7, Figure 14 p. 19).

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] Hallucinations are frequent overall: 440,445 of 2.23 million package mentions (19.7%) were hallucinated, including 205,474 unique non-existent names (p. 7).
2. [V] Commercial models hallucinated less than open models: GPT models 5.2% vs open-source 21.7% (p. 7). GPT-4 Turbo had the lowest rate at 3.59%. DeepSeek 1B was the lowest open model at 13.63% (p. 7). Per-model rates ranged up to 26.12% for Python (CodeLlama 7B) and 35.71% for JavaScript (CodeLlama 7B) (Tables 7–8, p. 20).
3. [V] Python hallucinated less than JavaScript: 15.8% vs 21.3% on average (p. 7). Stack Overflow prompts gave higher rates than LLM-generated prompts for almost every model, e.g. CodeLlama 7B Python 32.53% vs 21.51% (Table 7, p. 20).
4. [V] Hallucinations repeat within a model. Over 500 prompts re-queried 10 times each, 43% of hallucinated names reappeared in all 10 runs and 39% never reappeared. 58% reappeared more than once (p. 9).
5. [V] Most hallucinated names are model-specific: 81% of distinct names came from only one model (p. 10).
6. [V] Most hallucinated names are not typos of real packages. Only 13.4% (10,263 of 76,489) are within Levenshtein distance 1–2 of a real package; 48.6% are at distance 6 or more (p. 11).
7. [V] Deleted packages contribute almost nothing: 133 names (0.17%) matched packages removed from PyPI (p. 11). 8.7% (6,705 of 76,489) of hallucinated Python names are valid npm packages (p. 11).
8. [V] Temperature matters. Rates rise with temperature and jump above 1; at maximum temperature GPT-4 reached 8.9% and GPT-3.5 reached 31.8% (p. 8). Changing top-p/top-k/min-p increased rates slightly (+1.16% on average) and did not help (p. 8). Prompts on recent topics gave about a 10% higher rate (p. 8–9).
9. [V] Models can partly recognise their own hallucinations. GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-3.5 and DeepSeek detected them with accuracy above 75%. CodeLlama was biased toward labelling names as valid (Figure 7, Table 2, p. 10).
10. [V] All mitigations reduced hallucination rates (Table 4, p. 13). Fine-tuning reduced code quality: HumanEval pass@1 fell from 51.4% to 25.3% for DeepSeek and from 19.6% to 16.4% for CodeLlama (Table 5, p. 13).

| Condition | DeepSeek 6.7B | CodeLlama 7B |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline | 16.14% | 26.28% |
| RAG | 12.24% | 13.40% |
| Self-refinement | 13.04% | 25.51% |
| Fine-tuning | 2.66% | 10.27% |
| Ensemble | 2.40% | 9.32% |

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] The master list may already contain squatted hallucinated names, so the rates are a lower bound (p. 7).
- [A] RQ2–RQ4 were run only on Python, 4 models and sampled subsets. The authors argue this does not compromise generalisability (p. 7).
- [A] Newer models released since writing may behave differently. Few commercial models were tested because of funding (p. 13).
- [A] Self-refinement may misclassify valid packages as hallucinations (p. 12).
- [A] Fine-tuning reduces code quality (p. 13).
- [A] Removed-package lists are not fully disclosed by registries (p. 3). They did not publish real packages for ethical reasons, so exploitation was not demonstrated (p. 14).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **The metric mixes three name sources.** H2 and H3 ask the model directly for package lists (p. 6–7). Names from these answers are not necessarily names that would be installed from generated code. The pooled mention-level rate is therefore not the same quantity as "hallucinated dependency in code". It is also not comparable with rates computed by import/install parsing (e.g. churilov2026range) or per prompt (krishna2025importing). Based on the heuristic definitions on p. 6–7.
- [I] **Name normalisation and stdlib handling are not reported.** If names were matched without PEP 503 normalisation, case and separator variants of real packages would be counted as hallucinations, which would inflate rates. Based on the absence of any normalisation description on p. 7.
- [I] **Possible train/test leakage in the mitigation results.** Fine-tuning used the 560,000 valid responses produced from the same prompt datasets (p. 12–13). The prompts used to evaluate the fine-tuned models are not described. The 2.66% result may therefore be partly in-distribution.
- [I] **No uncertainty is reported.** Each condition is a single run. Rate differences of a few points (e.g. self-refinement on CodeLlama, 26.28% → 25.51%) cannot be judged without CIs (p. 13).
- [I] **Internal inconsistencies in the text and tables.**
  - 586,000 vs 576,000 samples (p. 2 vs p. 6).
  - CodeLlama is marked "✗" (not open source) in Table 1 (p. 6) but treated as open-source in the text.
  - Malformed counts in Table 7: "(2,495/41,7)" and "(2,8523/13,329)" (p. 20).
  - GPT-4 JavaScript SO cell: 3.86% does not equal 1,672/23,416 = 7.1% (p. 20).
  - The recency effect is phrased in both directions ("10% higher ... for older data versus more recent data" vs the summary "More recent prompting topics lead to a 10% increase", p. 8–9).

  These are probably typos, but they lower confidence in exact numbers.
- [I] **"10%" for recency is ambiguous.** It is not clear whether this means relative change or percentage points (p. 8).
- [I] **No real-world exploitation data.** The registry snapshot (January 2024) predates the analysis, and registrations of the hallucinated names after the run were not tracked (RQ2 gap).

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection):
  - [I] The same model both generates the code and names its packages (H2/H3), so its self-consistency is part of the measurement.
  - [I] Fine-tuning data comes from the same prompt pool used to evaluate it (p. 12–13).
  - [I] The LLM-generated prompts were produced by Llama-2 70B, which belongs to the same family as the CodeLlama models being evaluated (p. 5).
- External (generalisability of sample/context):
  - [I] Models date from 2023–early 2024 (p. 5–6). Agentic tools and IDE assistants are not covered.
  - [V] Only Python and JavaScript are studied (p. 6).
  - [I] Open models were run GPTQ-quantized (p. 6), so the results may not transfer to full-precision weights.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?):
  - [I] "Absent from the 10 Jan 2024 list" is used as a proxy for "hallucinated". The authors acknowledge the contamination direction (p. 7).
  - [I] Normalisation, stdlib handling and private or scoped names are unaddressed (p. 7).
  - [I] Mention-level counting gives more weight to verbose models.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No tests, no CIs, no repeated runs except the 10-run persistence check (p. 9). The large N makes the headline rates stable, but between-condition comparisons are not inferentially supported.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Prompts, system messages and parameters are given in Appendix B/C (p. 18–19), and code and datasets are public (p. 14). [V] The hallucinated-name list is withheld (p. 14). [I] Exact replication of the commercial-model results is impossible because those endpoints have since changed.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A] (p. 13):
  - Find the underlying causes of package hallucination: architecture, tokenizer, training-data composition.
  - Develop mitigations tailored to code: prompt engineering, knowledge graphs, loss refinement, new fine-tuning methods.
  - Add real-time feedback mechanisms.
  - Study persistence at the token level.
  - Develop fine-tuning that keeps code quality (p. 13).
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - Re-measure with an import/install-based extractor and explicit PEP 503 normalisation, so results are comparable with later studies.
  - Evaluate cheap tool-side defences on held-out prompts. Examples: a registry-existence plus package-age/popularity check before install, or self-refinement with a small model.
  - Track whether hallucinated names get registered over time (RQ2).

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (rates by model, language, temperature, recency), RQ2 (persistence, cross-model overlap, similarity to real names), RQ3 (RAG, self-refinement, fine-tuning), RQ4 (prompt sources, registry snapshot, heuristics).
- How it informs our work [I]:
  - **Baseline.** This is the baseline paper and the source of the reusable prompt corpus (public Zenodo/GitHub, p. 14). A laptop-scale study can sample from the SO and LLM-generated prompt sets and stay comparable with both this paper and churilov2026range.
  - **Replication details** (all from p. 5–7 and p. 18–19):
    - prompt sources: Stack Overflow top-20 per tag for 240 tags, 2023 vs pre-2023; Llama-2-70B prompts from top-5,000 package descriptions;
    - system prompts: Figures 10–13;
    - temperatures: 0.7 for code, 0.01 for package prompts;
    - registry snapshot: 10 Jan 2024;
    - metric: hallucinated / all recommended packages;
    - normalisation: not reported. Our study must define it explicitly (PEP 503 for PyPI, lowercase for npm, scoped names kept whole).
  - **Defences.** The two training-free mitigations are laptop-feasible: RAG over a package-description index (13.40% vs 26.28% on CodeLlama) and self-refinement. Self-refinement only helps models that can recognise their own hallucinations (p. 10, p. 13). Fine-tuning is costly and harmed code quality (p. 13).
  - **Persistence.** The 43%/39% split (p. 9) means a measurement study needs several samples per prompt to tell persistent names (worth squatting) from noise.
  - **Allow-list argument.** The authors argue that a plain existence check is insufficient because an attacker can pre-register names (p. 12). A lightweight defence should therefore add package age, popularity or provenance signals rather than existence alone.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)

## 14. Key quotes
> "the average percentage of hallucinated packages is at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models" (p. 1)

> "43% of hallucinated packages were repeated in all 10 queries, while 39% did not repeat at all across the 10 queries" (p. 9)

> "If a package name is not on the master list, it is considered a hallucination." (p. 7)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: Read the whole text: abstract, sections 1–7, ethics, open science, appendices A–G and Tables 6–8 (p. 1–20). The reference list was skimmed.
- Uncertainties:
  - The venue (USENIX Security '25) is not printed in the arXiv v3 text. It is taken from the project lead and the reference lists of churilov2026range and okwor2026hallucination.
  - Several figures (2, 3, 5–9) are plots. Their exact values could not be read from the text; only the numbers stated in the prose are used.
  - The table inconsistencies listed in section 9 were not resolved against the PDF images.

When I tried to write the first one (spracklen2024we) with the Write tool, the harness blocked it: "Subagents should return findings as text, not write report files." I did not try to get around the block with Edit or Bash, so all four files are still `status: draft` scaffolds. The complete analysis text for each key is below so you can write the files or ask the user to allow it.

What I could check:
- I confirmed 17 quotes and numbers on their cited pages using the `=== [PDF page N] ===` markers.
- I recomputed Krishna's p-values and Okwor's rule-of-three upper bounds (a quick 95% bound when zero events are seen: 3 divided by the sample size).

What I could not run:
- `rlab cite-check` and `rlab index`, because there was no file to check.

Each block below already says `status: ready`. After writing a file, run `python3 scripts/rlab.py cite-check 2026-11-12-package-hallucination-and-slopsquatting research/2026-11-12-package-hallucination-and-slopsquatting/papers/<key>/analysis.md`, then `rlab index`. If cite-check fails, set that file back to `draft`.

# Per-key summary

## spracklen2024we
- **Status:** ready (not written) · **evidence_basis:** full-text · tier 3 as analysed (arXiv v3, 2 Mar 2025, p. 1). The arXiv text does not name the USENIX Security '25 venue; I took it from your note and from the reference lists of churilov2026range (p. 16) and okwor2026hallucination (p. 9).
- **Summary:** 16 models from 2023–24 produced 576k Python and JavaScript code samples. 19.7% of 2.23M package mentions were hallucinated: 5.2% for commercial models vs 21.7% for open-source models (p. 7). Hallucinated names often repeat, and all three defences tested (retrieval of known package names, the model re-checking its own packages, fine-tuning) cut the rate, but fine-tuning lowered code quality.
- **Key findings:**
  - 440,445 of 2.23M mentions hallucinated; 205,474 unique names (p. 7).
  - 43% of hallucinated names come back in 10 of 10 re-runs, 39% never do (p. 9). 81% of names come from a single model (p. 10).
  - Only 13.4% are 1–2 edits from a real package name (p. 11). 8.7% of hallucinated Python names are real npm packages (p. 11).
  - Hallucination rises with temperature, sharply above 1; changing top-p, top-k or min-p does not help (p. 8).
  - Defences, Table 4 (p. 13), DeepSeek / CodeLlama: retrieval 16.14→12.24% / 26.28→13.40%; fine-tuning 2.66% / 10.27%, but HumanEval fell 51.4→25.3% for DeepSeek.
- **Doubtful:**
  - Name normalisation and standard-library handling are not reported.
  - The rate pools names the model gives when directly asked "which packages" (two of its three extraction methods) with install commands found in code (p. 6–7).
  - Fine-tuning used outputs from the same prompt pool; the evaluation prompts are not described, so leakage is possible.
  - No confidence intervals or significance tests.
  - Internal inconsistencies:
    - 586k vs 576k samples (p. 2 vs p. 6).
    - CodeLlama marked as not open-source in Table 1 (p. 6).
    - Malformed counts in Table 7 (p. 20).
    - GPT-4 JavaScript Stack Overflow cell says 3.86%, but 1,672/23,416 = 7.1%.
    - The recency effect is stated in both directions (p. 8–9).

## churilov2026range
- **Status:** ready (not written) · **evidence_basis:** full-text · tier 3. Single independent author; version 4, Nov 2026, which replaces all numbers of v1–3 and of the SCORED '26 workshop version (p. 1).
- **Summary:** A replication of Spracklen on 5 frontier models from 2026 (199,840 generations), with every name re-checked against the live registries under a plan registered in advance. Rates are 3.63–5.02% of package mentions; 104 names are hallucinated by all five models; about 1.1% of hallucinated names were registered within roughly six months.
- **Key findings:**
  - Mention-level rate 3.63–5.02%; generation-level rate 2.15–3.39% (p. 6). Python is higher than JavaScript for every model (p. 7).
  - Prompts written by an LLM give higher rates than Stack Overflow prompts: pooled 4.79/5.44% vs 2.28/3.10% (p. 7).
  - 104 names (88 PyPI, 16 npm) are hallucinated by all five models; 54 of them are one edit away from a registered package (p. 9). Mean name overlap between pairs of models (Jaccard similarity) is 0.219 (p. 8).
  - 25 of 2,282 hallucinated names were registered within about six months. Publishing names had no detectable effect (0/87 vs 2/101, p = 0.50). The test was underpowered: it could only detect a rise from 1% to about 10.5% (p. 12).
  - At least 23 names the models suggest had hosted malware that the registries later removed (p. 12). Re-checking against live registries lowered all earlier rates by about a fifth (p. 10).
- **Doubtful:**
  - It says "We follow Spracklen's extraction approach" (p. 5), but it parses import and install statements, which Spracklen explicitly rejects (spracklen p. 6). The headline comparison with 2024 therefore uses a different measure.
  - It credits Spracklen with two claims I could not find in Spracklen's text: npm "fragmentation" as the cause of higher JavaScript rates (p. 13), and "smaller models within a family tend to hallucinate more" (p. 9).
  - Temperature values are not printed (p. 4).
  - The registry checks were run in November 2026, about 6 months after generation (April 2026).
  - Many corrections between versions (p. 10–11). The author used Claude to write code and draft text (p. 15).
  - Prompt leakage: the Spracklen prompts were released in January 2025 and may be in the models' training data (p. 14).

## okwor2026hallucination
- **Status:** ready (not written) · **evidence_basis:** full-text · **tier 4** (single-author Zenodo preprint by an LLC; metadata shows a single source, no peer review).
- **Summary:** 5 local open-weight models run through Ollama produced 6,800 generations and 1,641 confirmed hallucinated names; none were registered when re-checked 4 days after the snapshot. Of 149 publicly listed hallucinated names, 22 are registered and none are malicious; 19 come from one anonymous operator registering harmless placeholder packages to block attackers.
- **Key findings:**
  - Snapshot t0 = 2026-06-30: 839,365 normalised PyPI names and 4,194,421 lowercased npm names, both pinned with SHA-256 hashes. A name counts only if it is absent from the snapshot AND the live registry returns 404 (p. 3).
  - The number of new names does not level off: 0.228 vs 0.247 new names per generation. 450 of the 455 new names came from a single model (p. 4).
  - 0 of 1,641 names registered on 2026-07-04; 95% upper bound below 0.2% (p. 5).
  - 22 of 149 public anchor names are registered: 19 placeholders, 1 organic name collision, 1 individual reservation, 1 typosquat from 2019, 0 malicious. 95% upper bound about 14% (p. 5–6).
  - Offline lab demo: code runs at install time on both ecosystems (pip via `setup.py`, npm via `postinstall`) (p. 7).
- **Doubtful:**
  - Printed DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21199427 (p. 1) differs from metadata ...426. This may be the Zenodo concept DOI vs a version DOI; not checked.
  - It cites Churilov's superseded v1–3 numbers (4.62–6.10%, 127 names, 53 registrable) and calls them "per generation". It also calls Spracklen's 21.7% "of generations" (p. 1–2), although both are mention-level rates.
  - No hallucination rate is reported.
  - Task set, prompts, seeds, hardware and the source of the import-to-package mapping are not reported.
  - The 4-day window for names that were never published makes the 0/1,641 result close to expected by design.
  - Code "will be deposited" (p. 8); it was not available.
  - One person assigned all intent labels.

## krishna2025importing
- **Status:** ready (not written) · **evidence_basis:** full-text · tier 3 (arXiv v1, 31 Jan 2025). Page 1 carries an ICML 2024 proceedings footer, which is almost certainly a template artefact because v1 was posted after ICML 2024; the venue is unverified.
- **Summary:** garak probes (an open-source tool for probing LLMs) tested 11 LLMs on JavaScript, Python and Rust prompts. The package hallucination rate, i.e. the share of prompts with at least one missing package, ranged from 0.22% to 46.15%: lowest for JavaScript, higher for Python and Rust. Bigger models and higher HumanEval scores go with lower rates, and a date-aware check is proposed as a defence but not evaluated.
- **Key findings:**
  - All 11 models hallucinate packages, 0.22–46.15% (Table 3, p. 4; p. 8). Mean rate: JavaScript 14.73%, Python 23.14%, Rust 24.74% (p. 8).
  - Definition is date-aware: a package registered after the model's knowledge cutoff, or less than 90 days before its release if the cutoff is unknown, counts as hallucinated (p. 3). Registry lists date from 30 January 2025 (p. 4).
  - Model size vs rate: r = −0.542, p = 0.00114 (p. 6). These p-values match n = 33 exactly (11 models × 3 languages treated as independent points); with n = 11, p ≈ 0.085, which is not significant (my recomputation).
  - HumanEval vs rate: r = −0.7887 on 10 models, no p-value reported (p. 7). Coding-specialised vs general models: no significant difference except for JavaScript (p. 6).
  - Prompts that ask for a non-existent package give "nearly double" the hallucinations of ordinary prompts; no numbers are given (p. 5).
- **Doubtful:**
  - Python imports are matched by regex with no reported import-to-package mapping (p. 12), so names like `sklearn` would likely be counted as hallucinated. The Rust `name::` path pattern would likely catch `std`/`crate`.
  - The claim that Mamba-Codestral beats its size class (p. 6) contradicts Table 5 (p. 7): Llama-3.1-8B averages 15.24% vs Mamba's 21.03%.
  - Coding-model statistics are internally inconsistent: a mean of 26.90% sits outside the stated range of 14.95–24.40% (p. 6).
  - Granite-3.0 is called "15 billion" in the text but listed as 8B in Table 1 (p. 6 vs p. 3).
  - The number of generations is not reported. My estimate is 7 × 13 × 3 × 5 = 1,365 per model, based on p. 4 and p. 12.
  - Temperature and decoding settings are not reported.
  - The abstract and introduction promise defences that were developed and evaluated (p. 1–2), but none is evaluated.
  - 3 of the 4 authors are at NVIDIA, NVIDIA's Nemotron model is the best performer, and there is no conflict-of-interest statement.
  - Prompt stubs include demographic personas ("As a woman", "a Black person") with no explanation (p. 12).
