  - 440,445 of 2.23M mentions hallucinated; 205,474 unique names (p. 7).
  - 43% of hallucinated names come back in 10 of 10 re-runs, 39% never do (p. 9). 81% of names come from a single model (p. 10).
  - Only 13.4% are 1–2 edits from a real package name (p. 11). 8.7% of hallucinated Python names are real npm packages (p. 11).
  - Hallucination rises with temperature, sharply above 1; changing top-p, top-k or min-p does not help (p. 8).
  - Defences, Table 4 (p. 13), DeepSeek / CodeLlama: retrieval 16.14→12.24% / 26.28→13.40%; fine-tuning 2.66% / 10.27%, but HumanEval fell 51.4→25.3% for DeepSeek.
- **Doubtful:**
  - Name normalisation and standard-library handling are not reported.
  - The rate pools names the model gives when directly asked "which packages" (two of its three extraction methods) with install commands found in code (p. 6–7).
  - Fine-tuning used outputs from the same prompt pool; the evaluation prompts are not described, so leakage is possible.
  - No confidence intervals or significance tests.
  - Internal inconsistencies:
    - 586k vs 576k samples (p. 2 vs p. 6).
    - CodeLlama marked as not open-source in Table 1 (p. 6).
    - Malformed counts in Table 7 (p. 20).
    - GPT-4 JavaScript Stack Overflow cell says 3.86%, but 1,672/23,416 = 7.1%.
    - The recency effect is stated in both directions (p. 8–9).

## churilov2026range
- **Status:** ready (not written) · **evidence_basis:** full-text · tier 3. Single independent author; version 4, Nov 2026, which replaces all numbers of v1–3 and of the SCORED '26 workshop version (p. 1).
- **Summary:** A replication of Spracklen on 5 frontier models from 2026 (199,840 generations), with every name re-checked against the live registries under a plan registered in advance. Rates are 3.63–5.02% of package mentions; 104 names are hallucinated by all five models; about 1.1% of hallucinated names were registered within roughly six months.
- **Key findings:**
  - Mention-level rate 3.63–5.02%; generation-level rate 2.15–3.39% (p. 6). Python is higher than JavaScript for every model (p. 7).
  - Prompts written by an LLM give higher rates than Stack Overflow prompts: pooled 4.79/5.44% vs 2.28/3.10% (p. 7).
  - 104 names (88 PyPI, 16 npm) are hallucinated by all five models; 54 of them are one edit away from a registered package (p. 9). Mean name overlap between pairs of models (Jaccard similarity) is 0.219 (p. 8).
  - 25 of 2,282 hallucinated names were registered within about six months. Publishing names had no detectable effect (0/87 vs 2/101, p = 0.50). The test was underpowered: it could only detect a rise from 1% to about 10.5% (p. 12).
  - At least 23 names the models suggest had hosted malware that the registries later removed (p. 12). Re-checking against live registries lowered all earlier rates by about a fifth (p. 10).
- **Doubtful:**
  - It says "We follow Spracklen's extraction approach" (p. 5), but it parses import and install statements, which Spracklen explicitly rejects (spracklen p. 6). The headline comparison with 2024 therefore uses a different measure.
  - It credits Spracklen with two claims I could not find in Spracklen's text: npm "fragmentation" as the cause of higher JavaScript rates (p. 13), and "smaller models within a family tend to hallucinate more" (p. 9).
  - Temperature values are not printed (p. 4).
  - The registry checks were run in November 2026, about 6 months after generation (April 2026).
  - Many corrections between versions (p. 10–11). The author used Claude to write code and draft text (p. 15).
  - Prompt leakage: the Spracklen prompts were released in January 2025 and may be in the models' training data (p. 14).

## okwor2026hallucination
- **Status:** ready (not written) · **evidence_basis:** full-text · **tier 4** (single-author Zenodo preprint by an LLC; metadata shows a single source, no peer review).
- **Summary:** 5 local open-weight models run through Ollama produced 6,800 generations and 1,641 confirmed hallucinated names; none were registered when re-checked 4 days after the snapshot. Of 149 publicly listed hallucinated names, 22 are registered and none are malicious; 19 come from one anonymous operator registering harmless placeholder packages to block attackers.
- **Key findings:**
  - Snapshot t0 = 2026-06-30: 839,365 normalised PyPI names and 4,194,421 lowercased npm names, both pinned with SHA-256 hashes. A name counts only if it is absent from the snapshot AND the live registry returns 404 (p. 3).
  - The number of new names does not level off: 0.228 vs 0.247 new names per generation. 450 of the 455 new names came from a single model (p. 4).
  - 0 of 1,641 names registered on 2026-07-04; 95% upper bound below 0.2% (p. 5).
  - 22 of 149 public anchor names are registered: 19 placeholders, 1 organic name collision, 1 individual reservation, 1 typosquat from 2019, 0 malicious. 95% upper bound about 14% (p. 5–6).
  - Offline lab demo: code runs at install time on both ecosystems (pip via `setup.py`, npm via `postinstall`) (p. 7).
- **Doubtful:**
  - Printed DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21199427 (p. 1) differs from metadata ...426. This may be the Zenodo concept DOI vs a version DOI; not checked.
  - It cites Churilov's superseded v1–3 numbers (4.62–6.10%, 127 names, 53 registrable) and calls them "per generation". It also calls Spracklen's 21.7% "of generations" (p. 1–2), although both are mention-level rates.
  - No hallucination rate is reported.
  - Task set, prompts, seeds, hardware and the source of the import-to-package mapping are not reported.
  - The 4-day window for names that were never published makes the 0/1,641 result close to expected by design.
  - Code "will be deposited" (p. 8); it was not available.
  - One person assigned all intent labels.

## krishna2025importing
- **Status:** ready (not written) · **evidence_basis:** full-text · tier 3 (arXiv v1, 31 Jan 2025). Page 1 carries an ICML 2024 proceedings footer, which is almost certainly a template artefact because v1 was posted after ICML 2024; the venue is unverified.
- **Summary:** garak probes (an open-source tool for probing LLMs) tested 11 LLMs on JavaScript, Python and Rust prompts. The package hallucination rate, i.e. the share of prompts with at least one missing package, ranged from 0.22% to 46.15%: lowest for JavaScript, higher for Python and Rust. Bigger models and higher HumanEval scores go with lower rates, and a date-aware check is proposed as a defence but not evaluated.
- **Key findings:**
  - All 11 models hallucinate packages, 0.22–46.15% (Table 3, p. 4; p. 8). Mean rate: JavaScript 14.73%, Python 23.14%, Rust 24.74% (p. 8).
  - Definition is date-aware: a package registered after the model's knowledge cutoff, or less than 90 days before its release if the cutoff is unknown, counts as hallucinated (p. 3). Registry lists date from 30 January 2025 (p. 4).
  - Model size vs rate: r = −0.542, p = 0.00114 (p. 6). These p-values match n = 33 exactly (11 models × 3 languages treated as independent points); with n = 11, p ≈ 0.085, which is not significant (my recomputation).
  - HumanEval vs rate: r = −0.7887 on 10 models, no p-value reported (p. 7). Coding-specialised vs general models: no significant difference except for JavaScript (p. 6).
  - Prompts that ask for a non-existent package give "nearly double" the hallucinations of ordinary prompts; no numbers are given (p. 5).
- **Doubtful:**
  - Python imports are matched by regex with no reported import-to-package mapping (p. 12), so names like `sklearn` would likely be counted as hallucinated. The Rust `name::` path pattern would likely catch `std`/`crate`.
  - The claim that Mamba-Codestral beats its size class (p. 6) contradicts Table 5 (p. 7): Llama-3.1-8B averages 15.24% vs Mamba's 21.03%.
  - Coding-model statistics are internally inconsistent: a mean of 26.90% sits outside the stated range of 14.95–24.40% (p. 6).
  - Granite-3.0 is called "15 billion" in the text but listed as 8B in Table 1 (p. 6 vs p. 3).
  - The number of generations is not reported. My estimate is 7 × 13 × 3 × 5 = 1,365 per model, based on p. 4 and p. 12.
  - Temperature and decoding settings are not reported.
  - The abstract and introduction promise defences that were developed and evaluated (p. 1–2), but none is evaluated.
  - 3 of the 4 authors are at NVIDIA, NVIDIA's Nemotron model is the best performer, and there is no conflict-of-interest statement.
  - Prompt stubs include demographic personas ("As a woman", "a Black person") with no explanation (p. 12).

# We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs

- Authors: Spracklen, Joseph; Wijewickrama, Raveen; Sakib, A H M Nazmus; Maiti, Anindya; Viswanath, Bimal; Jadliwala, Murtuza
- Year / venue: 2024, arXiv (preprint), analysed version arXiv:2406.10279v3, 2 Mar 2025 (p. 1). Published version: USENIX Security 2025. This is stated by the project lead and by the reference lists of two other project papers ([@churilov2026range, p. 16]; [@okwor2026hallucination, p. 9]). The arXiv text does not itself name the venue, so we analysed the arXiv text and cannot rule out differences from the proceedings version.
- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2406.10279 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10279
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
[A] The paper aims to quantify how prevalent package hallucinations are in Python and JavaScript code produced by commercial and open-source code LLMs, how model settings affect them, what the hallucinated names look like, and whether mitigation can reduce them without hurting code quality (p. 2, p. 4). The authors call it "the first systematic study" of package-hallucination frequency and nature (p. 2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [A] RQ1: how prevalent are package hallucinations in Python and JavaScript code generated by LLMs? (p. 4)
- [A] RQ2: how do model settings (training-data recency, temperature, decoding strategy) affect them? (p. 4)
- [A] RQ3: what model behaviours are observed: repetition within a model, cross-model repetition, verbosity, and self-detection? (p. 4)
- [A] RQ4: what properties do hallucinated names have: similarity to popular packages, cross-language confusion, and recently deleted packages? (p. 4)
- [A] RQ5: can RAG, self-refinement, decoding strategies or supervised fine-tuning mitigate hallucinations? (p. 4–5)
- [A] Explicit hypothesis on deleted packages: they expected a sizeable share of hallucinations to come from packages removed from PyPI. The hypothesis was not supported (p. 11).
- [A] Adversary model: the attacker can query the same LLMs, cannot modify them, finds hallucinated names by cross-referencing the registry and registers them. Victims install suggested packages without checking them (p. 4).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Three-phase pipeline: (i) build the prompt datasets, (ii) generate code, (iii) detect hallucinations (p. 5). This is followed by targeted sub-experiments for RQ2–RQ4 and a mitigation experiment for RQ5 (p. 7–13).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] 16 models (Table 1): GPT-4, GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-3.5 Turbo; CodeLlama 7B/13B/34B; DeepSeek Coder 1.3B/6.7B/33B; Magicoder 6.7B; WizardCoder 34B; Mistral 7B; Mixtral 8x7B; OpenChat 7B; WizardCoder-Python 7B; CodeLlama-Python 33B (p. 6). Selection used the top of the EvalPlus leaderboard as of 20 January 2024 plus the GPT models (p. 5). Two Python-only models were not tested on JavaScript, which gives 30 tests (p. 6).
- Package-name extraction: [V] Three heuristics (p. 6–7):
  - H1: parse `pip install` / `npm install` commands that appear in the output without being requested (7% of outputs).
  - H2: give the generated code back to the same model and ask for the list of packages needed to run it.
  - H3: give the original prompt back to the same model and ask which packages would solve the task.

  The authors explicitly reject parsing `import` / `require` because module names do not map uniquely to package names (p. 6, Appendix G p. 19).
- Hallucination decision: [V] A name is a hallucination if it is absent from a master list of PyPI or npm package names taken on 10 January 2024 (p. 7). [A] Because the master list may already contain squatted names, the authors present their rates as a lower bound (p. 7).
- Mitigation: [V] Three approaches, each tested alone and as an ensemble, on DeepSeek Coder 6.7B and CodeLlama 7B (p. 12–13):
  - RAG: 65,000 statements of the form "Package [x] could answer questions about [y]", generated with LlaMA-2 from the top 20,000 PyPI packages, stored in a vector DB, top-5 retrieved and appended to the prompt.
  - Self-refinement: the model is asked whether its packages are valid and regenerates up to 5 times.
  - Supervised fine-tuning: on 560,000 valid-only H1/H2 response pairs.
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Commercial vs open-source models; Python vs JavaScript; "recent" (2023) vs "all-time" (pre-2023) prompt subsets (p. 5, p. 7–8); temperature sweep and top-p/top-k/min-p settings (p. 8); unmitigated baseline vs each mitigation (p. 13). [V] They also compare their results with Lanyado's blog estimate (GPT-3.5 24.2%, GPT-4 22.2%) (p. 7).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] Stack Overflow dataset (p. 5):
  - 240 manually selected tags, each with more than 5,000 questions and relevant to Python or JavaScript.
  - The 20 most-upvoted questions per tag give 4,800 prompts per language.
  - This is done twice, once for 2023 ("recent") and once for before 2023 ("all-time"), giving 9,600 prompts per language.

  [V] LLM-generated dataset (p. 5):
  - Descriptions of the 5,000 most-downloaded PyPI and npm packages were turned into one-sentence coding prompts by Llama-2 70B (prompt template in Figure 13, p. 19).
  - About 4,800 prompts per language.
  - Also split into recent and all-time halves, with overlap removed.
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 19,200 code samples per model-language test, 30 tests, 576,000 code samples in total (p. 6). Two package prompts per sample give 1,152,000 package prompts (p. 7). These produced 2.23 million package mentions, of which 440,445 were hallucinated and 205,474 were unique hallucinated names (p. 7). [V] The paper also gives 19,500 prompts and 586,000 samples in the contributions list (p. 2), which does not match the 576,000 elsewhere (p. 1, p. 6). The source of this discrepancy is not reported.
- Sampling / selection method: [V]
  - RQ2–RQ4 use only Python, 4 models (GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-3.5, CodeLlama 7B, DeepSeek 6.7B) and "randomly sampled subsets" of the datasets (p. 7). The subset sizes are not reported, except for 500 prompts in the persistence test (p. 9).
  - Self-detection used randomly sampled valid and hallucinated names; the sample size is not reported (p. 9–10).
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Code, both prompt datasets, generated code, the RAG database and the fine-tuned models are released at Zenodo record 14676377 and GitHub Spracks/PackageHallucination (p. 2, p. 14). [V] The master list of hallucinated names and per-test detailed results are withheld and shared "by request to verified researchers" (p. 14).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
  - [V] Open-source models ran through Hugging Face transformers with GPTQ-quantized weights (p. 6).
  - [V] Hardware (p. 18): a 40-node Debian cluster with A100/V100 GPUs, and an Ubuntu machine with 3 RTX 6000 GPUs.
  - [V] RQ1 parameters (Table 6, p. 19): temperature 0.7 for code generation and 0.01 for package prompts; top-p 0.9; top-k 20; repetition penalty 1; max tokens 2048 for code and 64 for package prompts.
  - [V] System messages and prompts are given verbatim in Figures 10–13 (p. 18–19).
  - [V] Temperature sweep: up to 2 for GPT models and up to 5 for open-source models (p. 8).
  - [V] Decoding settings: top-p 0.4/0.6/0.8, top-k 5/10/15, min-p 0.1/0.2/0.3, plus one combined setting. Top-k and min-p were tested only on the open models (p. 8).
  - [V] Registry ground truth: PyPI and npm master lists as of 10 January 2024 (p. 7). Deleted packages were found with Google BigQuery PyPI download counts from 2022 and earlier (p. 11). Cross-language checks used libraries.io lists for 9 registries (p. 11).
  - **Name normalisation** (case folding, PEP 503 `-`/`_`/`.` equivalence, npm scopes): not reported.
  - **Standard-library exclusion**: not reported.
  - **Deduplication rule**: rates count mentions. "Unique" names are distinct strings (p. 7). The exact rule is not reported.
- Code availability: [V] Yes, see section 4 (p. 14).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - [V] Package hallucination rate = number of hallucinated packages / total recommended packages (p. 7). This is a mention-level rate. It pools names from H1 (installs inside code) and H2/H3 (the model answering a direct "which packages" question).
  - [V] Persistence: how many of 10 re-queries reproduce the same hallucinated name (p. 9).
  - [V] Number of models that generate each unique name (p. 10).
  - [V] Levenshtein distance to the nearest valid package (p. 10–11).
  - [V] Self-detection accuracy, precision and recall (p. 10).
  - [V] HumanEval pass@1 for code quality after fine-tuning (p. 13).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): Not reported. No confidence intervals, significance tests or variance across runs are given. Words such as "significantly reduce" are used descriptively (p. 1, p. 13). [V] The Python–JavaScript relationship is described as "linear" and "positively correlated" from a scatter plot. No coefficient is reported (p. 7, Figure 14 p. 19).

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] Hallucinations are frequent overall: 440,445 of 2.23 million package mentions (19.7%) were hallucinated, including 205,474 unique non-existent names (p. 7).
2. [V] Commercial models hallucinated less than open models: GPT models 5.2% vs open-source 21.7% (p. 7). GPT-4 Turbo had the lowest rate at 3.59%. DeepSeek 1B was the lowest open model at 13.63% (p. 7). Per-model rates ranged up to 26.12% for Python (CodeLlama 7B) and 35.71% for JavaScript (CodeLlama 7B) (Tables 7–8, p. 20).
3. [V] Python hallucinated less than JavaScript: 15.8% vs 21.3% on average (p. 7). Stack Overflow prompts gave higher rates than LLM-generated prompts for almost every model, e.g. CodeLlama 7B Python 32.53% vs 21.51% (Table 7, p. 20).
4. [V] Hallucinations repeat within a model. Over 500 prompts re-queried 10 times each, 43% of hallucinated names reappeared in all 10 runs and 39% never reappeared. 58% reappeared more than once (p. 9).
5. [V] Most hallucinated names are model-specific: 81% of distinct names came from only one model (p. 10).
6. [V] Most hallucinated names are not typos of real packages. Only 13.4% (10,263 of 76,489) are within Levenshtein distance 1–2 of a real package; 48.6% are at distance 6 or more (p. 11).
7. [V] Deleted packages contribute almost nothing: 133 names (0.17%) matched packages removed from PyPI (p. 11). 8.7% (6,705 of 76,489) of hallucinated Python names are valid npm packages (p. 11).
8. [V] Temperature matters. Rates rise with temperature and jump above 1; at maximum temperature GPT-4 reached 8.9% and GPT-3.5 reached 31.8% (p. 8). Changing top-p/top-k/min-p increased rates slightly (+1.16% on average) and did not help (p. 8). Prompts on recent topics gave about a 10% higher rate (p. 8–9).
9. [V] Models can partly recognise their own hallucinations. GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-3.5 and DeepSeek detected them with accuracy above 75%. CodeLlama was biased toward labelling names as valid (Figure 7, Table 2, p. 10).
10. [V] All mitigations reduced hallucination rates (Table 4, p. 13). Fine-tuning reduced code quality: HumanEval pass@1 fell from 51.4% to 25.3% for DeepSeek and from 19.6% to 16.4% for CodeLlama (Table 5, p. 13).

| Condition | DeepSeek 6.7B | CodeLlama 7B |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline | 16.14% | 26.28% |
| RAG | 12.24% | 13.40% |
| Self-refinement | 13.04% | 25.51% |
| Fine-tuning | 2.66% | 10.27% |
| Ensemble | 2.40% | 9.32% |

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] The master list may already contain squatted hallucinated names, so the rates are a lower bound (p. 7).
- [A] RQ2–RQ4 were run only on Python, 4 models and sampled subsets. The authors argue this does not compromise generalisability (p. 7).
- [A] Newer models released since writing may behave differently. Few commercial models were tested because of funding (p. 13).
- [A] Self-refinement may misclassify valid packages as hallucinations (p. 12).
- [A] Fine-tuning reduces code quality (p. 13).
- [A] Removed-package lists are not fully disclosed by registries (p. 3). They did not publish real packages for ethical reasons, so exploitation was not demonstrated (p. 14).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **The metric mixes three name sources.** H2 and H3 ask the model directly for package lists (p. 6–7). Names from these answers are not necessarily names that would be installed from generated code. The pooled mention-level rate is therefore not the same quantity as "hallucinated dependency in code". It is also not comparable with rates computed by import/install parsing (e.g. churilov2026range) or per prompt (krishna2025importing). Based on the heuristic definitions on p. 6–7.
- [I] **Name normalisation and stdlib handling are not reported.** If names were matched without PEP 503 normalisation, case and separator variants of real packages would be counted as hallucinations, which would inflate rates. Based on the absence of any normalisation description on p. 7.
- [I] **Possible train/test leakage in the mitigation results.** Fine-tuning used the 560,000 valid responses produced from the same prompt datasets (p. 12–13). The prompts used to evaluate the fine-tuned models are not described. The 2.66% result may therefore be partly in-distribution.
- [I] **No uncertainty is reported.** Each condition is a single run. Rate differences of a few points (e.g. self-refinement on CodeLlama, 26.28% → 25.51%) cannot be judged without CIs (p. 13).
- [I] **Internal inconsistencies in the text and tables.**
  - 586,000 vs 576,000 samples (p. 2 vs p. 6).
  - CodeLlama is marked "✗" (not open source) in Table 1 (p. 6) but treated as open-source in the text.
  - Malformed counts in Table 7: "(2,495/41,7)" and "(2,8523/13,329)" (p. 20).
  - GPT-4 JavaScript SO cell: 3.86% does not equal 1,672/23,416 = 7.1% (p. 20).
  - The recency effect is phrased in both directions ("10% higher ... for older data versus more recent data" vs the summary "More recent prompting topics lead to a 10% increase", p. 8–9).

  These are probably typos, but they lower confidence in exact numbers.
- [I] **"10%" for recency is ambiguous.** It is not clear whether this means relative change or percentage points (p. 8).
- [I] **No real-world exploitation data.** The registry snapshot (January 2024) predates the analysis, and registrations of the hallucinated names after the run were not tracked (RQ2 gap).

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection):
  - [I] The same model both generates the code and names its packages (H2/H3), so its self-consistency is part of the measurement.
  - [I] Fine-tuning data comes from the same prompt pool used to evaluate it (p. 12–13).
  - [I] The LLM-generated prompts were produced by Llama-2 70B, which belongs to the same family as the CodeLlama models being evaluated (p. 5).
- External (generalisability of sample/context):
  - [I] Models date from 2023–early 2024 (p. 5–6). Agentic tools and IDE assistants are not covered.
  - [V] Only Python and JavaScript are studied (p. 6).
  - [I] Open models were run GPTQ-quantized (p. 6), so the results may not transfer to full-precision weights.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?):
  - [I] "Absent from the 10 Jan 2024 list" is used as a proxy for "hallucinated". The authors acknowledge the contamination direction (p. 7).
  - [I] Normalisation, stdlib handling and private or scoped names are unaddressed (p. 7).
  - [I] Mention-level counting gives more weight to verbose models.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No tests, no CIs, no repeated runs except the 10-run persistence check (p. 9). The large N makes the headline rates stable, but between-condition comparisons are not inferentially supported.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Prompts, system messages and parameters are given in Appendix B/C (p. 18–19), and code and datasets are public (p. 14). [V] The hallucinated-name list is withheld (p. 14). [I] Exact replication of the commercial-model results is impossible because those endpoints have since changed.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A] (p. 13):
  - Find the underlying causes of package hallucination: architecture, tokenizer, training-data composition.
  - Develop mitigations tailored to code: prompt engineering, knowledge graphs, loss refinement, new fine-tuning methods.
  - Add real-time feedback mechanisms.
  - Study persistence at the token level.
  - Develop fine-tuning that keeps code quality (p. 13).
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - Re-measure with an import/install-based extractor and explicit PEP 503 normalisation, so results are comparable with later studies.
  - Evaluate cheap tool-side defences on held-out prompts. Examples: a registry-existence plus package-age/popularity check before install, or self-refinement with a small model.
  - Track whether hallucinated names get registered over time (RQ2).

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (rates by model, language, temperature, recency), RQ2 (persistence, cross-model overlap, similarity to real names), RQ3 (RAG, self-refinement, fine-tuning), RQ4 (prompt sources, registry snapshot, heuristics).
- How it informs our work [I]:
  - **Baseline.** This is the baseline paper and the source of the reusable prompt corpus (public Zenodo/GitHub, p. 14). A laptop-scale study can sample from the SO and LLM-generated prompt sets and stay comparable with both this paper and churilov2026range.
  - **Replication details** (all from p. 5–7 and p. 18–19):
    - prompt sources: Stack Overflow top-20 per tag for 240 tags, 2023 vs pre-2023; Llama-2-70B prompts from top-5,000 package descriptions;
    - system prompts: Figures 10–13;
    - temperatures: 0.7 for code, 0.01 for package prompts;
    - registry snapshot: 10 Jan 2024;
    - metric: hallucinated / all recommended packages;
    - normalisation: not reported. Our study must define it explicitly (PEP 503 for PyPI, lowercase for npm, scoped names kept whole).
  - **Defences.** The two training-free mitigations are laptop-feasible: RAG over a package-description index (13.40% vs 26.28% on CodeLlama) and self-refinement. Self-refinement only helps models that can recognise their own hallucinations (p. 10, p. 13). Fine-tuning is costly and harmed code quality (p. 13).
  - **Persistence.** The 43%/39% split (p. 9) means a measurement study needs several samples per prompt to tell persistent names (worth squatting) from noise.
  - **Allow-list argument.** The authors argue that a plain existence check is insufficient because an attacker can pre-register names (p. 12). A lightweight defence should therefore add package age, popularity or provenance signals rather than existence alone.

# The Range Shrinks, the Threat Remains: Re-evaluating LLM Package Hallucinations on the 2026 Frontier-Model Cohort

- Authors: Churilov, Aleksandr
- Year / venue: 2026, arXiv (preprint, not peer-reviewed). The analysed text is "Version 4 (November 2026)". It supersedes all numbers in versions 1–3 and in a SCORED '26 workshop version (p. 1). Single author, "Independent Researcher" (p. 1).
- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2605.17062 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17062
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
[A] To measure whether package hallucination has changed in the 2026 frontier-model cohort compared with Spracklen et al.'s 2024 baseline. Every name is revalidated against the live PyPI and npm registries. The paper also tests whether publishing hallucinated names speeds up their registration (p. 1–2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [A] Measurement question: has package hallucination changed for frontier models from 2025–26 (p. 1)? Main components:
  - per-model rates at the mention and generation levels;
  - the cross-model "universal" set and its registrability;
  - registration of hallucinated names (p. 2).
- [A] Preregistered hypothesis for the natural experiment: if publishing names attracts registrations, published names (group A) are registered more often than comparable unpublished names (group B4). The primary test is Fisher's exact test within strata of name frequency and name length (p. 11–12).
- [A] Threat model adopted from Spracklen. The attacker is an unprivileged actor who registers packages, and the attack has a 6-stage chain. The author estimates about $1,160 of API spend to enumerate names (p. 3).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Temporal replication with the same prompts and new models (p. 2, p. 4). Live-registry revalidation was preregistered on 7 Nov 2026, with a 20-entry deviation log (p. 6). The natural experiment uses an accidental public exposure of the universal list (p. 11).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Five models (Table 1, p. 4):
  - Claude Sonnet 4.6 (`claude-sonnet-4-6`)
  - Claude Haiku 4.5 (`claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`)
  - GPT-5.4-mini (`gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17`, reasoning effort minimal)
  - Gemini 2.5 Pro (`gemini-2.5-pro`)
  - DeepSeek V3.2 (alias `deepseek-chat`)

  No extended thinking was used for the Claude models (p. 4–5).
- Package-name extraction: [V] (p. 5)
  - `pip install` anywhere in a response, first argument only.
  - `npm install` inside code blocks only.
  - Import statements parsed with Python `ast` (sub-imports resolved to the top-level module) and tree-sitter for JavaScript.
  - Scoped npm names are kept whole.
  - requirements files, uv, poetry, yarn and pnpm are not extracted.
- Validation (p. 5): [V]
  - Two methods per registry: the PyPI JSON API and the Simple API (PEP 691); the npm registry document and deps.dev.
  - 200 = EXISTS, 404 = ABSENT, anything else = UNKNOWN.
  - A name is ABSENT only if both methods say ABSENT in two rounds at least 12 h apart: 7 Nov 2026 11:53–13:14 UTC and 8 Nov 2026 10:16–11:22 UTC.
  - Rate limit of 1 request/s per host; 14,821 requests with no errors.

  [V] Hallucination is judged as of generation time. The package creation time (npm `time.created`; PyPI earliest upload) is compared with the generation timestamp or the batch window. OSV is queried for malicious-package records (p. 5).
- Exclusions (p. 5–6): [V]
  1. Extraction noise.
  2. Standard library: the union of `sys.stdlib_module_names` for Python 3.10–3.13 and Node 18/20/22 built-ins.
  3. Names that fail PEP 508 or npm naming rules.
  4. Python import names that the pipreqs mapping links to an existing distribution. Names that appear as install targets stay candidates.
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Spracklen's 2024 numbers (3.59% best model; 5.2% commercial average; 21.7% open-source average) (p. 3, p. 6). Pairwise comparisons between the five models (p. 8). Earlier versions of the same study (p. 10–11).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] Spracklen's released prompt datasets, unmodified: 20,163 Stack Overflow prompts (SO_AT, SO_LY) and 19,806 LLM-synthesised prompts (LLM_AT, LLM_LY), split evenly between Python and JavaScript (p. 4). No new 2026 prompts were added (p. 4).
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V]
  - One sample per prompt per model: 39,969 generations per model (39,964 for Sonnet 4.6), 199,840 in total (p. 4).
  - Unique hallucinated names: PyPI 1,746 and npm 536 (Table 7, p. 11). Groups in the registration analysis: A = 104, B = 2,178 (p. 11–12).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] The models were chosen to represent the main commercial and open-weight providers at the frontier tier (p. 4). [A] The author says the selection is deliberate and that the results are conditional on it (p. 13).
- Data availability (public? link?): [V]
  - Code: GitHub `churik5/slopsquatting-replication-2026` (MIT).
  - Revalidation code, preregistration, deviation log and aggregate results: GitHub `churik5/slopsquatting-revalidation-2026`.
  - Raw responses (SQLite): available to verified researchers on request.
  - The universal list is not printed (p. 15).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
  - [V] Generations collected 22–28 April 2026 (p. 4, p. 14). Provider defaults were used "unless noted"; the actual temperature and top-p values are recorded but not printed in the paper (p. 4).
  - [V] Refusal rates range from 1.27% (Haiku 4.5) to 31.51% (GPT-5.4-mini) (Table 1, p. 4; p. 6).
  - [V] Estimated cost is $1,160.29 in total; the per-provider split is in Table A.1 (p. 17).
  - [V] Name normalisation for the Levenshtein analysis: "after normalization" against the registries' package lists of 23 July 2026. The normalisation rule itself is not specified (p. 9).
  - [V] PyPI validity uses PEP 508 and PEP 691. PEP 503 normalisation is not explicitly named (p. 5).
- Code availability: [V] Yes (p. 15). [A] The repository history was rewritten on 7 Nov 2026, so earlier commit references no longer resolve (p. 15).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - [V] Mention-level rate: share of extracted package references that are hallucinated. Chosen to match Spracklen's unit (p. 6).
  - [V] Generation-level rate: share of generations with at least one hallucinated reference; this is the preregistered rate (p. 6).
  - [V] Jaccard similarity of the unique hallucinated-name sets of each pair of models (p. 6).
  - [V] Registration share between exposure and T0 (p. 11).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V]
  - 95% Wilson CIs for rates.
  - Pearson χ² on 2×2 tables with Holm–Bonferroni correction across 10 pairs (α = 0.05).
  - Permutation tests with 10,000 resamples, seed 42 (p. 6).
  - Newcombe CIs for differences (p. 7, p. 12).
  - Fisher's exact test and Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel tests.
  - A stated minimum detectable effect: 10.5% at a 1% baseline with power 0.8 (p. 12).

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] Mention-level rates range from 3.63% (Haiku 4.5) to 5.02% (GPT-5.4-mini). Generation-level rates range from 2.15% (GPT-5.4-mini) to 3.39% (Gemini 2.5 Pro) (p. 6, Table 2 p. 7).
2. [V] 7 of 10 model pairs differ significantly at the mention level and 8 of 10 at the generation level. Gemini, DeepSeek and GPT-5.4-mini form a cluster with no significant differences (p. 6, Table 4 p. 8).
3. [V] Python rates exceed JavaScript rates for every model by 2.34–3.47 points per mention (Table 2, p. 7). [A] The author describes this as the reverse of Spracklen's 2024 pattern (p. 7, p. 13).
4. [V] LLM-synthesised prompts give higher rates than Stack Overflow prompts for every model. Pooled rates: 4.79% (LLM_AT) and 5.44% (LLM_LY) vs 2.28% (SO_AT) and 3.10% (SO_LY) (Table 3, p. 7).
5. [V] Overlap between models is moderate: mean Jaccard 0.219 (range 0.173–0.342). The DeepSeek V3.2 / GPT-5.4-mini pair is highest at 0.342 (p. 8).
6. [V] 104 names (88 PyPI, 16 npm) are hallucinated by all five models and account for 2,699 mentions. 54 of these names are one edit from a registered package. 4 are in npm scopes owned by organisations and cannot be registered by outsiders (Table 5, p. 9).
7. [V] Haiku 4.5 hallucinates less than Sonnet 4.6 (3.63% vs 4.09%, Holm p = 0.012). [A] The author withdraws an earlier explanation for this and has no mechanism (p. 9).
8. [V] Revalidation against live registries lowered every model's rate by about a fifth. Import names of real packages are the largest correction, at 144–207 mentions per model. The universal set fell from 127 to 104 names (p. 10–11, Tables 6–7).
9. [V] 25 of 2,282 hallucinated names (1.1%) were registered within about six months. Publication had no detectable effect: A vs B4 0/87 vs 2/101, difference −2.0 pp (95% CI −6.9 to +2.5), p = 0.50 (p. 12).
10. [V] Of the 24 registrations in group B, 22 are packages whose content was not inspected. One was an npm security-holding placeholder with a malicious-package record published after the runs, i.e. registered with malware and then removed. One is a name-reservation placeholder (p. 12).
11. [V] At least 23 names the models suggest had previously hosted malware that the registries removed: 13 npm security placeholders and 10 PyPI names with OSV malicious records (p. 12).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Scope: smaller open models, fine-tuned variants, quantized local checkpoints and agentic configurations are out of scope (p. 14).
- [A] Timing: generations from April 2026 and registry checks in November 2026 describe one point in time. Models change opaquely (p. 14).
- [A] Leakage: the Spracklen prompts were released in January 2025 and may be in 2026 pretraining data, which would bias rates downward. No held-out new prompts were used (p. 14).
- [A] GPT-5.4-mini ran at minimal reasoning effort and refused 31.51% of prompts; its compliant responses may not be a random subset (p. 14).
- [A] DeepSeek's alias returned `deepseek-v4-flash` metadata in the same window, so the underlying model may have changed (p. 14).
- [A] Extraction misses other install forms, so rates may be underestimated. The pipreqs mapping covers only about 1,157 import names (p. 14).
- [A] PyPI creation dates can be late if files were deleted. Removed malicious packages have no creation date (p. 14).
- [A] Registrability was not re-estimated (p. 14).
- [A] The natural experiment is small, detects only large effects, and cannot tell defensive from malicious registrations without inspecting content (p. 14).
- [A] Preregistration timestamps are self-attested, because the repository was local (p. 6, p. 14).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **The comparison with Spracklen uses a different construct.** The paper says "We follow Spracklen's extraction approach" (p. 5) but parses import statements. Spracklen explicitly rejects import parsing and instead asks the model for package lists ([@spracklen2024we, p. 6–7]). The mention-level rates therefore come from different extraction methods, and the headline "2026 frontier at 2024's commercial level" (p. 1, p. 6) is not a like-for-like comparison. The same applies to the Python>JavaScript "inversion" (p. 13). Based on comparing the method sections of both papers.
- [I] **Two claims are credited to Spracklen that we could not find there.** Churilov says Spracklen attributed higher JavaScript rates to npm's "larger and more fragmented namespace" (p. 13) and observed that "smaller models within a family tend to hallucinate more" (p. 9). A text search of spracklen2024we found neither statement.
- [I] **Residual import-name confusion may inflate Python rates.** pipreqs covers only about 1,157 names (p. 14), so uncovered module/distribution mismatches still count as hallucinations, and these occur mainly in Python. This could partly explain the Python>JavaScript result. The author's counter-argument is on p. 13.
- [I] **Long gap between generation and validation.** About 6 months passed between generation (April 2026) and the live checks (November 2026). The creation-time rule handles names registered in between (p. 5), but names deleted in between could be misclassified as hallucinations.
- [I] **The defaults are opaque.** Temperatures are not printed (p. 4), so the rates cannot be matched to Spracklen's temperature 0.7.
- [I] **Reliability record.** This is version 4 of a fast-revised, single-author paper with several non-reproducible earlier numbers (p. 10–11, p. 17). The text was drafted with AI help (p. 15). The transparency is commendable, but independent replication is needed before relying on exact values.
- [I] **Mention vs generation ordering depends on refusals.** GPT-5.4-mini's ranking flips between the two levels (p. 6), so "which model is safest" depends on how refusals are handled.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection):
  - [A] Possible training-data contamination with the prompt set (p. 14).
  - [I] Refusal behaviour differs between models and confounds generation-level rates (p. 6).
  - [I] Reasoning-effort and model-alias drift (p. 14).
- External (generalisability of sample/context):
  - [A] Results apply only to frontier API models; smaller or local models may still show 2024-like rates (p. 13–14).
  - [I] No agentic or IDE setting is covered.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?):
  - [I] Import-based extraction counts names in correct-looking code that may never be installed. Install targets are treated more strictly than imports (p. 5–6).
  - [V] A dated, two-method existence check is used (p. 5), which is stronger than earlier static lists.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance):
  - [V] Holm correction and permutation confirmation are used (p. 6, p. 8).
  - [V] The natural experiment is explicitly underpowered, with a minimum detectable effect of 10.5% (p. 12).
  - [I] One sample per prompt means within-prompt persistence is not measured.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Code, preregistration and aggregate results are public; raw responses are available on request (p. 15). [A] The repository history was rewritten and an earlier claim of a Zenodo deposit was incorrect (p. 15).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A] (p. 10, p. 13, p. 15):
  - Report cross-cohort intersections as a standard quantity (p. 10).
  - Make registration monitoring a standard part of measurement (p. 15).
  - Test smaller, quantized and next-tier models (p. 13–14).
  - Use held-out new prompts (p. 14).
  - Sweep reasoning effort (p. 14).
  - Study agentic configurations with retrieval (p. 14).
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - Re-run on laptop-scale open-weight models with the same live-validation protocol. This tier is explicitly out of scope here (p. 14).
  - Compare import-based and model-queried extraction on the same generations to make the 2024 and 2026 numbers comparable.
  - Measure persistence with k > 1 samples per prompt.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (frontier rates, language, prompt source, refusals), RQ2 (universal set, registrations, malware history), RQ4 (live two-method validation, time-of-generation rule, exclusions, statistics), RQ5 (scope gaps: local/quantized models, agents).
- How it informs our work [I]:
  - **Validation protocol.** This paper gives the most complete replicable protocol in the set:
    - two methods per registry: PyPI JSON plus Simple API; npm registry plus deps.dev;
    - two rounds at least 12 h apart;
    - 1 request/s per host;
    - append-only response log;
    - creation-time vs generation-time rule;
    - OSV malicious-record lookup;
    - stdlib exclusion via `sys.stdlib_module_names` and Node built-ins;
    - PEP 508 / npm naming-rule filter;
    - pipreqs import-to-distribution mapping;
    - Wilson CIs with Holm-corrected χ².

    All of this runs on a laptop (p. 5–6).
  - **Gap for a laptop study.** It explicitly leaves out quantized local checkpoints and agentic configurations (p. 14). That is directly the gap a laptop study can fill.
  - **Prompt bias.** LLM-synthesised prompts give roughly double the rates of SO prompts (p. 7), so a small study must stratify by prompt source.
  - **Defence design.** About 1% of hallucinated names get registered within 6 months, and at least 23 suggested names have a malware history (p. 12). A defence that only checks existence would therefore pass some dangerous names, which supports adding age, OSV or placeholder signals.

- Authors: Okwor, Daniel
- Year / venue: 2026, Zenodo preprint ("Preprint, July 2026"), single author, affiliation Orygn LLC (p. 1). **Source tier 4 (grey literature, not peer-reviewed); background evidence only.** Metadata verification is single-source (OpenAlex).

## 1. Research objective
[A] Prior work measures exposure, i.e. how often models hallucinate. This paper measures the next step, harm. It asks how many invented names are actually registered on the package index, by whom, and with what intent (p. 1–2). [A] The author claims that no prior work pulls true registration dates and adjudicates intent (p. 2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [A] Of the names models invent, how many are registered today? When a hallucinated name is registered, what is the claimant doing with it (p. 2)? No formal hypotheses are stated.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Two registration measurements plus a lab demonstration (p. 2):
  - (a) a self-generated corpus re-checked live;
  - (b) a public "anchor set" of previously reported names, adjudicated by registration date and static content;
  - (c) an offline install-time execution demo.
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Five open-weight models served via local Ollama: qwen2.5-coder:7b, deepseek-coder:6.7b, codellama:13b, codestral:22b and gpt-oss:20b (p. 3). Prompts ask for Python and JavaScript solutions across a "fixed task set" at temperatures 0.7 and 1.0, with fixed seeds. gpt-oss gets a larger output budget (p. 3).
- Hallucination gate ("two-oracle"): [V] (p. 3)
  - Oracle A: the name is absent from a frozen snapshot taken at t0 = 2026-06-30. PyPI: 839,365 normalised names from the simple index. npm: 4,194,421 lowercased names from a public name mirror. Both lists are hashed with SHA-256.
  - Oracle B: the name returns a live 404.
  - Absent at t0 but live now = candidate post-t0 registration. Present at t0 but 404 now = yanked package. Network error = unknown.
- Extraction: [V] (p. 3)
  - Python is parsed with `ast`; JavaScript with acorn plus a lenient fallback.
  - Import names are mapped to distribution names (e.g. sklearn → scikit-learn); the source of the mapping is not reported.
  - PEP 503 normalisation.
  - Standard-library and built-in modules excluded.
  - Scoped and subpath specifiers resolved.
  - Names that fail the registries' name-shape rules are dropped.
- Anchor-set adjudication: [V] (p. 4)
  - True first-registration time: npm `time.created`; PyPI minimum release upload time.
  - Static triage only: read `setup.py`, `PKG-INFO` and manifests as text, looking for install hooks and red-flag tokens.
  - Fixed rubric: malicious / defensive placeholder / organic / individual reservation.
- Baselines or comparison conditions: None. [V] There is a negative control: names absent from the snapshot but live in the extra run (p. 7).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] The self-generated corpus (p. 3–4). [V] The anchor set: 149 previously published hallucinated names from the Trend Micro slopsquatting dataset and the DepScope corpus (p. 2–4). How the 149 were chosen from those datasets is described only as names "that have circulated long enough to attract registration" (p. 1, p. 5). The selection rule is not reported.
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 4,800 generations, then 2,000 more with fresh seeds, 6,800 in total. These gave 1,186 + 455 = 1,641 distinct confirmed hallucinated names (p. 4). Anchor set: 149 names, of which 22 are registered (p. 5).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Balanced round-robin across the five models (p. 5, Figure 1). The task set size, prompt texts and per-language split are not reported.
- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Code, configuration and snapshot hashes "will be deposited" with a DOI (p. 8). The raw name list is withheld. Registry metadata behind the attribution analysis is available to reviewers under embargo (p. 9). Not available at the time of writing.

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
  - [V] Temperatures 0.7 and 1.0, fixed seeds, Ollama runtime (p. 3).
  - Seeds, max tokens, quantization levels of the Ollama models, and hardware: not reported.
  - [V] Live re-check of all 1,641 names on 2026-07-04 (p. 5). The date of the anchor-set registration check is not reported.
  - [V] Gate validation on a holdout of 17 known-real and 8 synthetic fake names: precision and recall 1.000 (p. 4). [A] "Every headline count" was re-derived by an independent recomputation (p. 4); the procedure is not described.
- Code availability: Not yet available (p. 8).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - [V] Count of distinct confirmed hallucinated names, and new names per generation, used as a saturation measure (p. 4).
  - [V] Share of names registered, with a rule-of-three 95% upper bound (p. 5–6).
  - [V] Taxonomy of registered names by intent (p. 5–6).
  - Not reported: any hallucination rate, at either the mention or the generation level.
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] Rule-of-three upper bounds only: below 0.2% for 0/1,641, about 14% for 0/22, about 2% for 0/149 (p. 5–6). No other tests.

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] The space of invented names does not saturate. The marginal yield was 0.228 new names per generation in the extra run vs 0.247 in the original. 450 of the 455 new names came from a single model (p. 4). 82 of the first 1,186 names were produced by two or more models (p. 4).
2. [V] All 1,641 self-generated hallucinated names were still unregistered on 2026-07-04; the 95% upper bound is below 0.2% (p. 5).
3. [V] Of 149 public anchor names, 22 are registered: 19 defensive research placeholders, 1 organic collision, 1 individual reservation, 1 pre-AI typosquat from 2019, and 0 malicious. The 95% upper bound on the malicious fraction is about 14% (p. 5–6).
4. [V] The 19 placeholders share an identical summary ("Benign slopsquatting research package") and blank identity fields. They were uploaded by numbered aliases of one operator, consistent with working around a per-account rate limit (p. 6).
5. [V] Negative control: 11 names absent from the snapshot but live at check time all predate t0 (2014–2023). They are npm mirror misses, not new squats (p. 7).
6. [V] In an offline lab, a benign package executed code at install time on both pip (`setup.py` during build) and npm (`postinstall`) before any import (p. 7).
7. [V] The npm name mirror is unreliable: it lists more names than npm's own total yet misses real old packages (p. 3).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Zero malicious is not zero risk. "Benign now" is version-scoped, because a placeholder can be weaponised in a later release (p. 8).
- [A] The registered census is small (22 of 149) and biased toward defender-claimed names, because defenders scrape the same public lists. One adjudicator assigned the intent labels (p. 6, p. 8).
- [A] The corpus is a lower bound, because npm mirror false inclusions reject some real hallucinations before the live check (p. 3, p. 8).
- [A] The corpus is self-generated, not production or agent traffic (p. 8).
- [A] The time window is short (p. 7–8).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **The "cleanest result" is close to guaranteed by design.** The 1,641 names were generated privately and re-checked 4 days after the snapshot (p. 5). An attacker could only have registered them by independently generating the same names within days. The 0/1,641 result therefore says little about attacker behaviour. Based on the dates on p. 3 and p. 5.
- [I] **No hallucination rate is reported.** Neither mentions per generation nor share of generations is given, so RQ1 cannot use this paper. The models and prompts are under-specified: the task set, prompts and quantization are unknown.
- [I] **Cited numbers are misreported.**
  - Spracklen's 21.7% is described as "of generations" (p. 1). Spracklen defines the rate per recommended package ([@spracklen2024we, p. 7]).
  - Churilov's "4.62% to 6.10% per generation", "127 names" and "53 registrable" (p. 1–2) are version 1–3 numbers. Churilov's version 4 supersedes them (3.63–5.02% of mentions, 104 names, registrability not re-estimated) ([@churilov2026range, p. 10–11]), and those earlier rates were mention-level.
- [I] **The anchor-set selection is opaque.** How 149 names were drawn from the datasets is not specified (p. 4–5), and the date of the registration check is not given.
- [I] **Static triage of `setup.py`, `PKG-INFO` and manifests may miss payloads** located in package modules or loaded at import time. Wheels-only packages are not discussed (p. 4).
- [I] **Possible conflict of interest is not addressed.** The author's affiliation is a company (Orygn LLC, p. 1); no funding or conflict-of-interest statement is given.
- [I] **Results are not reproducible until the promised deposit appears** (p. 8).

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection):
  - [A] The anchor set over-represents defender-claimed names (p. 6).
  - [I] There is a single adjudicator (p. 8) and the rubric is applied without inter-rater checks.
- External (generalisability of sample/context):
  - [A] Small local open-weight models only; not agent traffic (p. 8).
  - [I] PyPI and npm only.
  - [I] One snapshot in mid-2026.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?):
  - [I] "Unregistered after 4 days" does not measure exploitability.
  - [V] The two-oracle gate (absent at t0 AND live 404) is a sound definition of hallucination at t0 (p. 3).
  - [I] It ignores whether a name was hallucinated relative to the model's training cutoff (cf. krishna2025importing).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [V] Only rule-of-three bounds are reported (p. 5–6). [I] With 22 registered names the malicious-share bound (~14%) is wide; the author acknowledges it rules out only a high rate (p. 6).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?):
  - [V] Snapshot hashes are promised (p. 3).
  - [I] Prompts, seeds and the task set are not given.
  - [A] Code is not yet deposited (p. 8).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A] (p. 8):
  - Keep the 1,641-name corpus under prospective watch with periodic re-checks.
  - Move to live coding-agent traffic.
  - Obtain larger gated corpora not pre-filtered by public visibility.
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - Report hallucination rates with denominators.
  - Publish the prompt set.
  - Re-check registrations at 3, 6 and 12 months.
  - Inspect wheel contents as well as setup files.
  - Combine with Churilov's six-month registration data for a longer baseline.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (registration and intent of hallucinated names; defensive squatting), RQ4 (frozen hashed snapshot plus live gate; import-to-distribution mapping), RQ5 (local Ollama setting; agent traffic as future work).
- How it informs our work [I]:
  - **Closest template for a laptop-scale measurement.** Five open-weight models run locally through Ollama (p. 3). The pipeline uses:
    - a frozen, SHA-256-hashed registry snapshot (PyPI simple index, PEP 503-normalised; npm names lowercased) as an offline pre-filter;
    - a live-404 confirmation;
    - `ast`/acorn parsing;
    - import-to-distribution mapping;
    - stdlib exclusion (p. 3).
  - **Known pitfall.** The npm name mirror is unreliable (p. 3). Treat the live registry as ground truth, or use npm's replication feed.
  - **Replication gaps.** The task set, prompts, seeds and hardware are missing, so the setup cannot be copied exactly.
  - **Evidence weight.** Its registration findings complement churilov2026range (about 1% registered in six months, one with malware). Both suggest weaponised slopsquatting on PyPI/npm is still rare. As tier-4 evidence this paper should only corroborate, not anchor, RQ2 claims.

# Importing Phantoms: Measuring LLM Package Hallucination Vulnerabilities

- Authors: Krishna, Arjun; Galinkin, Erick; Derczynski, Leon; Martin, Jeffrey (University of Waterloo; NVIDIA) (p. 1)
- Year / venue: 2025, arXiv (preprint, not peer-reviewed), arXiv:2501.19012v1, 31 Jan 2025 (p. 1). Page 1 carries the footer "Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, Vienna, Austria. PMLR 235, 2024" (p. 1). [I] This is most likely an ICML template artefact: v1 was posted in January 2025, after ICML 2024. The venue is treated as unverified.
- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2501.19012 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19012
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index). PDF pages 13–23 are only figure-placeholder stubs.

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
[A] To measure package hallucination across programming languages (Python, JavaScript, Rust) and LLM types, find patterns linking model characteristics to hallucination, and develop defensive strategies (p. 1–2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [A] RQ1: how often does package hallucination happen? (p. 2)
- [A] RQ2: what impact does the programming language have? (p. 2)
- [A] RQ3: how does model size affect it? (p. 2)
- [A] RQ4: does it differ between coding-specialised and general-purpose LLMs? (p. 2)
- [A] Also investigated: "induced" hallucination (asking for a non-existent package or API) vs "natural" hallucination (p. 3, p. 5).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Black-box probing with the garak framework. Prompts are posed, imported packages are extracted from the output, and the names are compared against the registry lists (p. 3).
- Definition: [V] A package hallucination is a package that meets one of the following (p. 3):
  - it is not registered in npm / PyPI / crates.io; or
  - it was first registered after the model's knowledge cutoff; or
  - if the cutoff is unknown, it was first registered less than 90 days before the model's first publication.

  How the knowledge cutoffs were obtained is not reported.
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] 11 models (Table 1, p. 3):
  - CodeGemma 7B
  - Dracarys-Llama-3.1-70B
  - GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06)
  - Granite-3.0 8B
  - Llama-3.1 8B and 70B
  - Mamba-Codestral 7B
  - Mistral-NeMo-Minitron-8B
  - Llama-3.1-Nemotron-70B
  - Qwen2.5-Coder 7B
  - StarCoder2-15B

  Six are classed as code-specialised and five as general-purpose (p. 6). Open-weight models were preferred (p. 3–4).
- Prompts: [V] Every combination of 7 request stubs and 13 coding-task descriptions, filled in for each language (p. 4; Tables 6–7, p. 12). Each request is repeated five times (p. 4). The stubs include persona variants ("As a woman, I need example...", "What <language> module would a Black person use...") (p. 12). Their purpose is not explained. Which prompts count as "induced" is not stated explicitly.
- Extraction: [V] Regular-expression extractors (p. 12):
  - Python: `import x`, `from x import`, `import x as`.
  - JavaScript: ES6 `import ... from`, CommonJS `require()`.
  - Rust: `use x`, `extern crate x`, and `x::` path references.

  Mapping from import name to distribution name, normalisation and standard-library exclusion: not reported.
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Comparisons across languages, code vs general models, model size, and HumanEval/MBPP scores (p. 4–7). No mitigation baseline.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] Registry scrapes of package names and release dates. Counts as of 30 January 2025: npm 3,391,235; PyPI 604,814; crates.io 169,823 (Table 2, p. 4). The scraping method is not reported.
- Sample size (N) and unit: The number of generations per model or in total is not reported. [I] From the design we estimate 7 stubs × 13 tasks × 3 languages × 5 repeats = 1,365 prompts per model, about 15,000 in total (p. 4, p. 12). This is our estimate, not a reported figure. The model sample is 11 (p. 6).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Models chosen to vary in size, provider and purpose (p. 3). The tasks are a hand-picked mix that includes niche or possibly fictional targets: "StrombergDB", "Tektronics 4051", "Query/400" (p. 12).
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Only a generic statement that the work used open-source software and openly available models (p. 10). No dataset or code link is given in the paper.

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] garak orchestration (p. 3); 5 repeats per request (p. 4). Temperature, decoding settings, max tokens, hardware, inference provider and model quantization are not reported.
- Code availability: No repository is linked in the paper (p. 10). [I] garak itself is open source; whether the exact probe used is included in it is not stated.

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] Package Hallucination Rate (PHR) = the proportion of prompts that produced at least one hallucinated package (p. 4). This is a generation-level rate, unlike Spracklen's per-package rate. Repetition and varied prompts are used to reduce fragility (p. 4).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V]
  - Pearson correlation between size and PHR: r = −0.542, p = 0.00114; with ln(size): r = −0.593, p = 0.00028 (p. 6–7).
  - HumanEval vs PHR: r = −0.7887. MBPP vs PHR: r = −0.2919. No p-values for these (p. 7).
  - T-test, code vs non-code: significant only for JavaScript; no significant difference once GPT-4o is removed (p. 6).

  No CIs for PHR. No multiple-comparison correction.

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] Every model hallucinated packages in every language. PHR ranged from 0.22% (Nemotron-Llama-3.1-70B, JavaScript and Rust) to 46.15% (Granite-3.0, Python) (Table 3, p. 4; p. 8).
2. [V] Mean PHR by language: JavaScript 14.73%, Python 23.14%, Rust 24.74% (p. 8; Figure 1, p. 5). Variance across models is highest for Python (σ = 16.03), then Rust (14.37), then JavaScript (8.43) (p. 4).
3. [V] GPT-4o PHR: JavaScript 1.76%, Rust 10.99%, Python 3.52%. Nemotron-70B: 0.22%, 0.22%, 4.84% (Table 3, p. 4).
4. [V] Larger models hallucinate less: r = −0.542, p = 0.00114 (p. 6). [I] These p-values are reproduced exactly by n = 33, i.e. 11 models × 3 languages treated as independent points. With n = 11 models the same r gives p ≈ 0.085 (raw) or ≈ 0.055 (log). The size effect is therefore not significant at the model level. Based on our recomputation of the t-test for a correlation coefficient.
5. [V] Higher HumanEval scores go with lower average PHR: r = −0.7887 over 10 models (Dracarys has no score) (Table 5, p. 7). [A] The authors say coding benchmarks "can serve as efficient proxies for assessing hallucination risks" (p. 7).
6. [V] Code-specialised models have higher mean PHR: Python 30.22% vs 14.64%, Rust 31.58% vs 16.53%, JavaScript 18.90% vs 9.71% (Table 4, p. 6). The difference is significant only for JavaScript and disappears without GPT-4o. [A] The authors conclude there is likely no meaningful distinction (p. 6).
7. [A] Induced hallucinations occur at "nearly double" the rate of natural ones. No numbers are given, and the authors note that there were far fewer induced attempts (p. 5).
8. [A] Proposed mitigation: a date-aware verification list of packages published before each model's training cutoff, used to flag suggestions. Developers should prefer familiar packages and name packages explicitly (p. 8). This is not evaluated.

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] The sample of 11 models may be too small to detect a code vs non-code difference (p. 6).
- [A] There are far fewer induced attempts than natural ones (p. 5).
- [A] Training-data composition is unavailable, so ecosystem-size and popularity explanations remain speculative (p. 5).
- [A] The verification-list approach does not address malicious packages already in the historical index (p. 8).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **Likely false positives from module/package mismatch.** Python imports are extracted by regex with no reported import-to-distribution mapping or stdlib filter (p. 12). Common module names that differ from their PyPI distribution (e.g. `sklearn`, `cv2`, `yaml`) and stdlib modules may be counted as hallucinations. The Rust `name::` pattern can match `std::`, `crate::` or local modules. This would inflate the Python and Rust PHR. Compare churilov2026range, which found import names of real packages to be the largest false-positive class ([@churilov2026range, p. 10]).
- [I] **Pseudo-replication in the size correlation.** See finding 4. The headline "statistically significant" size effect depends on treating language results of the same model as independent.
- [I] **Text contradicts the paper's own tables.**
  - "Mamba-Codestral ... achieving lower PHRs than all other models in its size class" (p. 6), but Table 5 gives Mamba-Codestral 21.03% vs Llama-3.1-8B 15.24% (p. 7).
  - Coding models are said to span "14.95% to 24.40% PHR ... µ = 26.90%" (p. 6); a mean cannot lie outside its range.
  - Granite-3.0 is described at "15 billion parameter scale" (p. 6) but listed as 8B (p. 3).
- [I] **Key quantities are missing.** The number of generations, temperature, the source of the cutoff dates and the classification of induced prompts are all not reported. Induced vs natural rates have no numbers.
- [I] **The defence is not evaluated.** The abstract and introduction say the work develops and evaluates defensive strategies (p. 1–2), but the mitigation section (p. 8) only proposes one.
- [I] **The task set is tiny and idiosyncratic.** 13 hand-picked tasks, several referring to obscure or fictional systems (p. 12), make PHR highly task-dependent. Results are not comparable in magnitude with Spracklen or Churilov.
- [I] **Undisclosed potential conflict of interest.** Three of four authors are at NVIDIA (p. 1), two NVIDIA-derived models are evaluated, and Nemotron performs best. No conflict-of-interest statement is given.
- [I] **Unexplained demographic prompt stubs** (p. 12) add uncontrolled variance.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] The task choice drives rates. Mixing induced and natural prompts in one PHR confounds the two constructs (p. 4–5, p. 12).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] 11 models from 2024 with a small prompt grid. [V] This is the only study in the set that covers Rust/crates.io (p. 4).
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?):
  - [V] The date-aware definition is a distinctive strength: it counts post-cutoff registrations, including possible squats, as hallucinations (p. 3).
  - [I] Regex import extraction without mapping weakens construct validity.
  - [I] Generation-level PHR differs from Spracklen's mention-level rate.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] Pseudo-replicated correlations; no CIs; HumanEval correlation over 10 points with no p-value (p. 6–7).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] The prompt stubs and tasks are listed in full (p. 12). [I] Decoding settings, generation counts and code are not reported, so exact replication is not possible.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A] (p. 6, p. 8–9):
  - Reduce package hallucination in smaller models.
  - Study the link between code optimisation and security.
  - Build defences that work across languages and architectures.
  - Test whether non-transformer (Mamba) architectures are more robust.
  - Use more models to test the coding vs general difference.
  - Use multi-objective optimisation of coding quality vs PHR (p. 7).
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - Implement and evaluate the proposed date-aware verification list, which is cheap and laptop-feasible.
  - Re-run with import-to-distribution mapping and stdlib filtering.
  - Report the generation counts and model-level statistics.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (language incl. Rust, model size, coding vs general, induced vs natural), RQ3 (proposed date-aware verification list), RQ4 (date-aware definition, registry snapshot, PHR metric, regex extraction), RQ5 (untested defence).
- How it informs our work [I]:
  - **Ready-made laptop tooling.** It uses garak (open source) and small models in the 7–8B range (p. 3), so the measurement harness can run on a laptop.
  - **Two reusable ideas.**
    - (a) The date-aware hallucination definition, which ties registry release dates to each model's knowledge cutoff (p. 3), helps catch names squatted after training.
    - (b) The induced-prompt condition (p. 3, p. 5) is a cheap stress test.
  - **The proposed date-aware verification list (p. 8) is untested.** Evaluating it, alongside age, popularity and OSV checks, as a client-side pre-install filter is a concrete candidate defence for our implementation study.
  - **Replication details to copy, and to fix.**
    - Copy: prompt grid (Tables 6–7, p. 12); registry snapshot 30 Jan 2025 (p. 4); PHR per prompt (p. 4); 5 repeats (p. 4).
    - Fix: add import-to-distribution mapping, PEP 503 normalisation and stdlib filtering; report N; analyse at the model level.

## spracklen2024we — ready-quality content, NOT WRITTEN · full-text · tier 3 as analysed
Analysed arXiv v3 (2 Mar 2025, p. 1). The arXiv text does not name the USENIX Security '25 venue; your note and the reference lists of churilov2026range (p. 16) and okwor2026hallucination (p. 9) do.

**Summary:** 16 models from 2023–24 produced 576k Python/JS code samples, and 19.7% of 2.23M package mentions were hallucinated (5.2% commercial vs 21.7% open-source) (p. 7). Hallucinated names often repeat, and retrieval, self-checking and fine-tuning all cut the rate; fine-tuning also lowered code quality.

**Key findings:**
- 440,445 of 2.23M mentions hallucinated; 205,474 unique names. GPT-4 Turbo lowest at 3.59%. JavaScript 21.3% vs Python 15.8% (p. 7).
- 43% of hallucinated names reappear in 10 of 10 re-runs and 39% never do (p. 9). 81% of names come from only one model (p. 10).
- Only 13.4% are 1–2 edits from a real package. 8.7% of hallucinated Python names are real npm packages. Deleted PyPI packages explain 0.17% (p. 11).
- Rates rise with temperature, sharply above 1. Changing top-p, top-k or min-p does not help (+1.16%) (p. 8).
- Defences, Table 4 (p. 13), DeepSeek / CodeLlama:
  - Retrieval of known package names: 16.14→12.24% / 26.28→13.40%.
  - Self-refinement (model re-checks its own packages): 13.04% / 25.51%.
  - Fine-tuning: 2.66% / 10.27%, but HumanEval fell 51.4→25.3% / 19.6→16.4%.

**Details for a replication:**
- Prompts: Stack Overflow, top 20 questions per tag for 240 tags, 2023 vs pre-2023; plus Llama-2-70B prompts generated from descriptions of the top 5,000 packages. Released on Zenodo 14676377 / GitHub (p. 5, p. 14).
- System prompts: Figures 10–13 (p. 18–19).
- Settings: temperature 0.7 for code and 0.01 for package lists; top-p 0.9; top-k 20 (p. 19). Open models were GPTQ-quantized (p. 6).
- Registry snapshot: master lists from 10 Jan 2024 (p. 7).
- Extraction: install commands in code plus two prompts asking the model for package lists. Import parsing is explicitly rejected (p. 6).
- Metric: hallucinated mentions / all recommended packages.
- Not reported: name normalisation, standard-library handling, statistics.

**Doubtful:**

- Fine-tuning data came from the same prompt pool; the evaluation prompts are not described, so leakage is possible.
- No confidence intervals.
- Inconsistencies:

## churilov2026range — NOT WRITTEN · full-text · tier 3
Single independent author. Version 4 (Nov 2026) replaces all numbers in v1–3 and in a SCORED '26 workshop version (p. 1).

**Summary:** A replication of Spracklen on 5 frontier models from 2026 (199,840 generations), with every name re-checked against the live registries under a plan registered in advance. Rates are 3.63–5.02% of package mentions; 104 names are hallucinated by all five models; about 1.1% of hallucinated names were registered within roughly six months.

**Key findings:**
- Rates: 3.63–5.02% of mentions and 2.15–3.39% of generations; 7 of 10 model pairs differ significantly (p. 6–8).
- Python > JS for every model by 2.34–3.47 points (p. 7). LLM-written prompts give higher rates than Stack Overflow prompts: 4.79/5.44% vs 2.28/3.10% (p. 7).
- 104 names hallucinated by all five models (88 PyPI, 16 npm); 54 are one edit from a real package. Mean name overlap between pairs of models (Jaccard similarity) is 0.219 (p. 8–9).
- 25 of 2,282 names (1.1%) were registered within about six months. Publishing names had no detectable effect (0/87 vs 2/101, p = 0.50), but the test could only detect a rise from 1% to about 10.5% (p. 12).
- At least 23 names the models suggest had hosted malware that registries removed (p. 12). Live re-checks lowered all earlier rates by about a fifth; import names of real packages were the largest correction (p. 10–11).

**Details for a replication:**
- Models and snapshot IDs: Table 1 (p. 4). Generations were collected 22–28 Apr 2026.
- Temperatures: "defaults", values not printed (p. 4).
- Extraction: `pip install` (first argument only), `npm install` inside code blocks, imports via Python ast / tree-sitter (p. 5).
- Registry checks: two methods per registry (PyPI JSON plus Simple API; npm registry plus deps.dev), two rounds on 7 and 8 Nov 2026 at least 12 h apart, 1 request/s per host. A name counts as hallucinated if it did not exist when generated. OSV is queried for malware records (p. 5).
- Exclusions:
  - standard library (`sys.stdlib_module_names` for Python 3.10–3.13; Node 18/20/22 built-ins);
  - names invalid under PEP 508 / npm rules;
  - import names mapped to real packages via pipreqs (p. 5–6).
- Statistics: Wilson CIs; chi-square with Holm correction; permutation tests (seed 42) (p. 6).
- Cost: $1,160 (p. 17).

**Doubtful:**
- It says "We follow Spracklen's extraction approach" (p. 5), but it parses imports, which Spracklen explicitly rejects (spracklen p. 6). The 2024 vs 2026 comparison and the "Python > JS inversion" therefore use different measures.
- It credits Spracklen with two claims I could not find in Spracklen's text: npm "fragmentation" as the cause of higher JS rates (p. 13), and "smaller models hallucinate more" (p. 9).
- The pipreqs mapping covers only about 1,157 names (p. 14), so some Python false positives remain.
- Many corrections between versions (p. 10–11). Text drafted with Claude (p. 15).
- Prompts may be in the models' training data (p. 14). The DeepSeek alias may have changed model during the run (p. 14).
- Small, quantized local models and agentic setups are explicitly out of scope (p. 14).

## For a laptop-scale study
- **Okwor** is the closest template: local Ollama models, a hashed snapshot plus a live 404 check.
- **Churilov** gives the most complete validation protocol, and it explicitly leaves out local quantized models and agents.
- **Spracklen** provides the public prompt corpus and two cheap, training-free defences (retrieval of known package names; self-refinement).
- **Krishna** provides garak tooling and an untested date-aware verification-list defence, which is a candidate for implementation.
